World.title: Experimental skin cream linked to 2-year drop in biological age in early study
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

An experimental skin cream altered molecular markers associated with aging and inflammation in an early human trial, according to preliminary data released by its developer this week.

Rubedo Life Sciences, a biotechnology company based in Mountain View, California, tested its investigational treatment, RLS-1496, in patients with eczema and other skin conditions.

In an analysis of 11 paired skin samples from patients with atopic dermatitis, researchers reported that four weeks of treatment was associated with an average 2.1-year decrease in measured epigenetic skin age, an estimate based on age-related changes in DNA.

3 COMMON FACTORS MAY BE SECRETLY SPEEDING UP THE AGING PROCESS, EXPERT SAYS

Rubedo CEO Dr. Frederick Beddingfield said the "significant" early findings warrant further investigation.

"This is one of the few drugs developed for aging in general and with AI to show positive data in humans in multiple indications and to show a reduction in skin age," Beddingfield told Fox News Digital.

He believes the early results will translate into "clinical improvements with longer-term treatment."

The latest skin-aging findings have been presented at a scientific conference but have not yet been published as a full peer-reviewed study.

SCIENTISTS UNVEIL 'LIVING BANDAGE' THAT COULD DRAMATICALLY SPEED WOUND HEALING

RLS-1496 is designed to target senescent cells, aging or damaged cells that have stopped dividing but can release substances that promote inflammation.

The drug targets a protein called GPX4, which helps cells respond to stress. Researchers are studying whether blocking it can clear away damaged, aging cells while helping healthier cells survive.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Beddingfield described the approach as targeting cellular aging rather than simply treating its outward effects.

"It's a bit like 'what does not kill you makes you stronger' for those surviving cells," he added.

Skin samples showed a 10% increase in a type of collagen that helps support the skin, according to the company. Blood tests also showed lower levels of several markers linked to inflammation, although it is not yet clear what those changes mean for patients' health.

CLICK HERE TO 

The preliminary findings come with several limitations. The skin-aging analysis included just 11 paired samples and measured biological signs of aging in the skin rather than whether the skin actually looked younger or functioned better.

Treatment lasted only four weeks, so it is not known whether the changes will persist. The studies were sponsored by Rubedo, and the latest skin-aging findings have not yet been published as a full peer-reviewed study.

"Our next trial will treat for several months," Beddingfield said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The treatment is also being tested for other skin issues. In a separate early-stage study of 22 patients with actinic keratosis, rough, precancerous skin patches caused by sun exposure, the company reported a 49% average reduction in lesions after 28 days of treatment.

The open-label study compared treated forearms with untreated forearms rather than a placebo cream.

The cream caused minimal skin irritation, and the drug was detected in the blood of very few participants, according to the company.

"With topical application, we have seen very little risk," Beddingfield said. "Local irritation is rarely seen and generally mild when it occurs, and no one has discontinued treatment to date. Very few subjects show any drug in their blood after skin application."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Rubedo is also beginning an early-stage trial of RLS-1496 for androgenetic alopecia, or pattern hair loss.

Beddingfield estimated that potential FDA approval remains three to four years away, pending larger clinical trials.

World.title: Can cooking for terrorists bar asylum? Supreme Court takes up unusual case with broader immigration stakes
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A Nigerian man forced to cook thousands of meals for the Unknown Gunmen, a militant group linked to political violence in Nigeria, is at the center of a Supreme Court showdown that could determine how broadly immigration authorities can apply a terrorism-related bar to asylum and how far the Trump administration can go in deporting immigrants accused of supporting terrorism.

The Supreme Court agreed Tuesday to hear the Trump administration's challenge to a ruling that overturned Nigerian citizen Izuchukwu Ozurumba's deportation order, setting up a legal battle over whether ordinary services provided to terrorist organizations, including cooking meals, can disqualify immigrants from receiving asylum even when those services are not directly connected to terrorist attacks.

Ozurumba was deported to Nigeria in April 2025 while his appeal was pending.

THE SUPREME COURT IS BACK; THESE FIVE CASES COULD RESHAPE AMERICAN LIFE

At the center of the case is a provision of the Immigration and Nationality Act that bars certain immigrants who provide "material support" to terrorist organizations from receiving asylum. The law lists examples of prohibited assistance, including transportation, communications, housing, money, weapons and training, but it does not explicitly define what constitutes material support.

"The biggest takeaway is that this is a case about who gets to draw the line on a law that affects national security," Bryce Poole, a senior legal fellow with Advancing American Freedom, told Fox News Digital. "Congress wrote a broad rule, and the court interpreted it narrowly."

The case also comes two years after the Supreme Court overturned Chevron deference, a legal doctrine that required judges to defer to federal agencies' reasonable interpretations of ambiguous laws. The 2024 ruling gave judges greater authority to decide what those laws mean.

The 4th Circuit, in a 2-1 ruling, overturned Ozurumba's deportation order and sent the case back to the Board of Immigration Appeals.

Judge James Wynn Jr., an Obama appointee, wrote the majority opinion, joined by Judge Nicole Berner, a Biden appointee. The judges concluded that, although Ozurumba prepared thousands of meals for the group's leaders, his cooking did not provide resources that could be directly used or readily redirected toward terrorist operations.

Although Ozurumba said he was forced to cook under threat of violence, the 4th Circuit did not decide whether the law contains an exception for assistance provided under duress, an issue the court previously addressed in a 2012 ruling that relied on Chevron deference. Instead, the majority found that his cooking for the terrorist organization did not qualify as "material support" that would bar him from asylum, leaving the separate duress question unresolved.

The Trump administration argued that the 4th Circuit interpreted the law too narrowly, insisting that even ordinary services such as cooking meals can help sustain a terrorist organization and free its members to carry out attacks.

"Because he's cooking the meals, one of the armed guards doesn't have to cook the meals and can be an armed guard," Poole said.

"That's one guard who doesn't have to come in off guard duty to cook meals, or that's one bomb maker who doesn't have to stop making bombs to go cook meals, because all this stuff is fungible."

Ozurumba said he initially agreed to work as a chef at a "rural camp," preparing three meals a day for 15 to 17 leaders. He later learned the camp belonged to the Unknown Gunmen.

An immigration judge determined that the Unknown Gunmen qualified as a "Tier III" terrorist organization under federal immigration law, even though the State Department had not formally designated the group as one.

Ozurumba said armed guards prevented him from leaving. According to court records, he cooked for the group's leaders for roughly six months, including three months without pay, before escaping during a trip into town to buy groceries.

STATE'S LARGEST MOSQUE LEADER’S DEPORTATION FIGHT TAKES DRAMATIC TURN AS TRUMP ADMIN SCORES MAJOR WIN

Ozurumba said members of the Unknown Gunmen continued threatening and attacking him after his escape, prompting him to flee Nigeria for Venezuela and eventually the United States. He crossed the southern border without valid entry documents in July 2023 during the Biden administration and surrendered to Border Patrol agents.

An immigration judge denied Ozurumba's asylum request and ordered his deportation, a decision upheld by the Board of Immigration Appeals after finding that his cooking violated the federal material-support rule. The 4th Circuit later rejected that interpretation and sent the case back to the immigration board.

Judge Julius Richardson disagreed with the majority, arguing in his dissent that cooking thousands of meals for terrorist leaders freed them to focus on their organization's goals and therefore constituted material support.

"Ozurumba did not run a hot dog stand that the Unknown Gunmen happened to stop by once or twice," Richardson wrote. "Rather, he acted as a private chef, providing three meals a day for over a dozen leaders of a terrorist organization — for months."

Hans von Spakovsky, a legal expert with Advancing American Freedom, also argued that the majority misinterpreted the law.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

"The idea that providing over 8,000 meals for the leaders of a terrorist organization and its members is not 'material' defies common sense," von Spakovsky told Fox News Digital. "Richardson correctly cites Napoleon’s famous quote that an 'army marches on its stomach.'

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Other federal appeals courts have all held that providing food and shelter, even if unconnected to a specific terrorist event, constitutes material support within the statute," von Spakovsky continued. "And doing so under duress, even if true, is not an excuse under the statute to avoid removal."

Even if the Supreme Court rules in his favor, a victory would not automatically grant him asylum or guarantee his return to the United States. His case would still need to be reconsidered by immigration authorities.

The 4th Circuit previously declined to order the government to bring him back, instead leaving it up to officials to decide whether his presence in the U.S. would be necessary for further proceedings.

World.title: Feds investigate suspicious letters sent to lawmakers and election officials
World.content:
WASHINGTON — Federal law enforcement is investigating dozens of letters containing suspicious substances mailed to congressional offices and state election officials across the country less than three weeks before Election Day.

Three law enforcement sources briefed on the matter told NBC News that preliminary testing of the white powder substance showed that the contents are not hazardous. However, additional testing will continue at law enforcement labs around the country to ensure the letters do not contain anything dangerous.

The offices of several Democratic senators, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York, were targeted. Election offices in at least 15 states — Arizona, Delaware, Georgia, Idaho, Kansas, Louisiana, Nebraska, New Hampshire, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Dakota, Tennessee, Washington and Wisconsin — said they were mailed suspicious packages.

The FBI, U.S. Capitol Police and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service were looking into the mailings, according to a notice sent to senior staff members in Senate offices Thursday.

“Law enforcement officials are working to intercept any additional letters before they are delivered, however, it is possible that some letters may reach their destinations,” the notice said, according to two people who received it.

Two law enforcement sources briefed on the matter confirmed that “dozens of letters” were sent, but because law enforcement continues to intercept the letters, they declined to put an exact number on how many have been received or seized.

A letter with a suspicious substance was addressed to Schumer and intercepted by authorities, a spokesperson for Schumer said.

An office for Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., was also targeted, a spokesperson for Padilla told NBC News, adding that the FBI notified the office that a letter containing a suspicious substance was intercepted by the U.S. Postal Service.

A letter with a suspicious substance was also sent to Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy’s office in Hartford, Connecticut, his spokesperson, Josh Sorbe, said in a statement. The FBI, Capitol Police and the sergeant at arms informed the office about the letter, Sorbe said, adding that Murphy and his staff “were not in immediate danger.”

The Postal Inspection Service and Capitol Police referred questions from NBC News to the FBI, which confirmed in a statement that the agencies are investigating “a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices.” It did not specify the locations of the targeted offices.

“Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident,” the statement said. “We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters.”

Former FBI Supervisory Special Agent Jason Pack told NBC News that even if the letters are not hazardous or they turn out to be a hoax, there is still a possible crime and the investigation will continue.

“There’s several different statutes that may come into play here, whether that’s mailing a threat or mailing something believed to be a hazardous substance,” he said. “And that could be five to 20 years behind bars.”

Pack said the Postal Inspection Service, along with the FBI, has developed good expertise in investigating suspicious letters over the years. Federal agents know how to trace mail from its origin.

“They’ll be able to go back and do investigations based on where these pieces of mail originated and then work backwards,” he said. “In pretty short order, I would think [they would] find out at least a bit more information about who sent it.”

He said that though the motive was unclear, “the timing is somewhat suspicious with the election ahead of us.”

Election Day is Nov. 3, but early voting is already underway in numerous states.

The notice Senate staffers received Thursday included an image of one of the suspicious envelopes and said the letters “may contain different variations of postage stamps.” It also warned that suspicious letters, packages or substances “should be treated as potentially hazardous and handled in accordance with established safety protocols.”

The notice outlined how staffers should handle the items and noted that mail and packages delivered to Senate offices or the Capitol complex are screened and tested for potential threats.

The House sergeant at arms sent a similar notice to House lawmakers and staff members Thursday. It said that while mail and packages delivered to the House offices in the Capitol are rigorously screened, district offices should use safe mail handling procedures, including using “mail hoods” — screening equipment that allows handling mail without exposing staff members to danger — provided by the sergeant at arms, according to two congressional offices who shared the message with NBC News. The notice said no House members had been identified as intended recipients of the mailings.

The notice sent to Senate staffers did not say whether the congressional offices involved are the ones in Washington, D.C., or local and regional offices. Congress is on recess leading up to the midterm elections, so most lawmakers are back home in their districts as they campaign in the final weeks before Election Day. Congressional staff members, however, are still on the Capitol campus.

NBC News reported Wednesday that state election offices in Louisiana, Ohio and Oklahoma were sent packages this week containing mysterious powders. Oklahoma and Louisiana reported receiving the envelopes, while Ohio said U.S. Postal Service investigators intercepted a package destined for it.

Threats against election workers have increased in recent years, including incidents of suspicious substances’ being mailed to their offices. It happened in 2023 and just weeks before the presidential election in 2024.

CORRECTION (Oct. 15, 2026, 5:23 p.m. ET): A previous version of this article misidentified which Oklahoma office received a package. It was the state Election Board, not the secretary of state’s office. The article also mischaracterized election oversight in Oklahoma. That is carried out by the Election Board, not the secretary of state.

World.title: Kevin Warsh speech could offer clues on whether Fed will raise interest rates this month
World.content:
When Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh strides onstage in Bangkok on Friday morning, it will be after 11 p.m. on Thursday in New York. But investors, economists and politicians in the United States will be awake and hanging on his every word.

Any speech by a Fed chair is closely scrutinized. This week’s talk has an extra dose of urgency, though, after two government reports showed inflation heating up for consumers and businesses — spurring speculation about how soon the Fed will raise interest rates to handle soaring prices.

Warsh will be speaking at the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, where he will be interviewed by IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva. The Fed chairman has repeatedly said he will not use public speaking engagements to intentionally steer the expectations of investors and markets, but his comments could nevertheless signal whether the central bank will hike rates before, or after, the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

It will also be the last speech from a Fed official before policymakers enter a “blackout” period on Saturday that lasts through their next interest rate meeting, which is scheduled for Oct. 27 and 28.

“Broad based” inflation “strengthens the case for an October hike,” Bank of America analysts wrote on Wednesday. “The data continue to underscore two key sources of inflation pressure: AI and Iran.”

Those two factors aren’t likely to be going anywhere soon, either.

The price of politics

Already hammered by soaring interest rates, rising energy prices and stagnant wage growth, American consumers could get an extra dose of financial strain if the Fed raises rates again this month.

Voters are already dissatisfied with President Donald Trump’s handling of the economy, polls show, so another rate hike could add to Republicans’ headaches as they face potentially losing their congressional majorities in the midterms.

In recent weeks, Trump has tried to pull multiple policy levers to lower gas and diesel prices, which have pushed inflation higher in recent months. But none of them have yet slowed prices meaningfully.

“Starting on day one, we will end inflation and make America affordable again,” Trump said on the campaign trail in 2024. Inflation as measured by the consumer price index declined to as low as 2.3% four months into Trump’s term.

But that same month, Trump unleashed a wave of tariffs across the globe, dramatically changing the economic story.

By September, inflation breached the 3% threshold again. In February, Trump launched the war against Iran, causing one of the worst energy supply shocks in history. Inflation jumped as high as 4.1% in May, and looks to be headed back in that direction again.

Another Fed rate hike would also further undermine Trump’s yearslong pressure campaign to push the central bank to cut rates. Since Warsh took his post in May, the central bank has either held rates steady or increased them.

Trump hasn’t attacked Warsh after years of hammering former Chair Jerome Powell. But the president has started saying that the other members of the Fed’s board are “very hostile.”

“I’m relying on Kevin,” Trump told reporters in September, “but he’s got, you know, a very tough board. He’s got a board that was put there by a lot of other people, and the interest rates are too high.”

“They’re very political,” Trump said. Four of the Fed’s seven board members were appointed by Trump.

Asked what the president’s expectations are for Warsh’s appearance, the White House pointed to a Truth Social post from September in which Trump had written, “Interest rates in the United States should be 1% or less.”

Diesel and the damage done

Economists and investors are paying close attention to so-called core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices. Both reports this week showed that even this adjusted measure of price growth is running hotter than hoped for.

“Core CPI was the more significant surprise,” wrote analysts at Bank of America.

The core readings showed that skyrocketing fuel prices, particularly diesel, are trickling down. Farmers, truckers and others who keep commerce humming in the United States have to raise their prices in order to digest higher diesel costs. That, in turn, leads to price increases for consumer goods.

“The cost of diesel gets into just about everything,” KPMG chief economist Diane Swonk told NBC News in an August interview. “Everything from … running a farm … cost of food, but also everything across the economy that’s shipped gets that extra fee tacked onto it.” At the time, she described the surge in diesel fuel prices as likely “an inflationary problem for the next several months.”

Her warning came to fruition in September, according to the consumer price index and producer price index reports this week. With diesel prices remaining solidly above $6 per gallon so far in October, and with no sign that the Iran war is near an end or that attacks on energy assets in the Ukraine-Russia war will be paused, it could keep fueling overall inflation for months.

Big Tech is also fueling inflation. Trillion-dollar companies are spending, and borrowing, big sums for servers, memory and other components that will be used in data centers. That’s caused price spikes across the economy.

Companies including Apple and Nintendo have raised prices as a result. “We have never seen a component price increase this much, this quickly,” Apple told NBC News in June.

Companies are also tapping the public debt markets in an unprecedented way. Data center companies and associated utility firms, chipmakers and cloud providers are expected to raise between $300 billion and $570 billion from the debt market this year, according to Vanguard. Those firms are also offering highly attractive interest rates, sometimes better than U.S. Treasury bonds.

A consequence of that, Warsh noted recently, is that there’s a “competition for capital” driving up interest rates on government debt, too.

“This is a complicated set of things that are affecting the most important asset anywhere in the world, the 10-year Treasury,” Warsh said. “It’s the risk-free asset upon which every price of virtually every asset in the world is related to.”

Without referencing the Iran war, he also said yields were being driven by “geopolitics” and the strength of the economy.

World.title: ICE agent driving vehicle that struck and injured Houston man is placed on administrative leave
World.content:
The ICE officer accused of running over an immigrant in Houston on Saturday has been put on administrative leave while the incident is investigated, a senior Department of Homeland Security official told NBC News.

As NBC News has reported, a senior DHS official said that multiple ICE officers on the scene at the time were wearing body cameras and that ICE is reviewing video of the scene as part of an internal investigation.

The DHS official said no decision has been made about sharing the video with the public or with the Harris County District Attorney’s Office, which is conducting its own investigation.

District Attorney Sean Teare told NBC News on Thursday that he has interviewed a key witness who was handcuffed in the back of the ICE vehicle when it hit Miguel Parra Hernández. The witness “had a front-row seat to the incident and everything that led up to it,” Teare said. “We did get a significant amount of relevant details from him.”

The witness was interviewed at the Port Isabel Processing Center, about 35 to 40 miles from the U.S.-Mexico border in South Texas, according to the district attorney’s office. The Port Isabel facility is historically known as the last stop before an immigrant is removed from the U.S.

Teare said his office is compiling all information it has gathered or is still gathering, and “in very short order we’re going to come to a point where we present this to a grand jury.” He said that could happen as soon as next week.

Security video shows the moment an ICE vehicle struck a man in Houston. KPRC

Teare and Cesar Espinosa, co-founder and executive director of FIEL Houston, an immigrant civil rights group, identified the witness as José Presa Cañada.

“It’s very troubling” that Presa is in Port Isabel, Espinosa said Thursday. “We want to know why he’s there and why he hasn’t been released yet and why they are trying to deport him so expeditiously.”

Teare declined to comment on what was said during the interview with Presa. Teare also has interviewed Parra.

The auto-pedestrian collision Saturday, which left Parra hospitalized with multiple injuries and needing surgery, triggered the investigation, which could result in charges of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, according to Teare.

The district attorney’s office said it notified ICE soon after the incident that it wanted to interview Presa. In an email, ICE responded that Teare should get to Port Isabel fast because the agency planned to deport Presa, according to the district attorney’s office.

ICE did not immediately respond to a request for information about its detention of Presa and whether it plans to deport him.

ICE has said Parra was not its arrest target on Monday. An agency spokesperson said Parra ran into the ICE vehicle’s path.

The other potential witness who was handcuffed in the ICE vehicle that hit Parra is Luis Delfín Martínez, who is being held in the Montgomery Processing Center in Conroe, north of Houston, according to advocates and relatives.

Miguel Parra Hernández. Courtesy FIEL

The district attorney’s office has issued subpoenas for Parra’s medical records, as well as for records of emergency medical personnel who responded when Parra was struck.

Teare, Parra’s attorney Kim Bruno and advocates have been pressing the Trump administration not to deport Parra and the two men in the vehicle and have asked the district attorney and others to protect them.

Teare said in an interview this week that his office had been in touch with consulates for the countries of origin of all three men to let them know it was ready to assist with their applications for visas for witnesses key to criminal cases, known as U visas.

“We’re working with the powers that be in a really significant effort to keep them here in this country,” he said then.

Teare told NBC News that it’s “pretty obvious” from videos his office has collected, including drone video, that ICE intentionally hit and ran over Parra, an allegation ICE has said is reckless and false.

Security video of the incident obtained by NBC affiliate KPRC of Houston shows a white truck facing the opposite direction of traffic on a busy roadway. Parra and another man exit the white truck and run, the video shows.

At about the same time, the video shows, another vehicle jumps a yellow median and heads in Parra’s direction. The video then shows the vehicle, which is not marked, swerving left toward Parra’s path, in front of a truck stopped in a shopping center.

When the parked truck leaves, a man can be seen lying on the pavement behind the ICE vehicle, the video shows.

Teare sought to download data from the ICE vehicle while it was still at the scene, but an agent drove the car away. Driving the car may have automatically erased critical data, said Teare, who led the district attorney’s office’s vehicular crimes division for several years.

World.title: Cornell president faces contentious faculty senate meeting over Jane Doe allegations
World.content:
Cornell University’s president was met with scrutiny and sharp questions from its faculty senate Wednesday, when the group convened to discuss a no-confidence vote over the university’s handling of an alleged 2024 sexual assault at a fraternity house, according to an audio recording obtained by NBC News.

Discussion of a no-confidence vote comes after serious concerns were raised by students and staff over how the university responded to the allegations.

University President Michael Kotlikoff defended himself and Cornell’s administration as he took a series of pointed questions from the school staff.

At the meeting, most speakers were heard identifying themselves before speaking. Risa Lieberwitz, a professor of labor and employment law, said the issue of sexual assault “is a systemic problem. It deserves systemic attention.”

She told Kotlikoff that thus far it appeared he had “simply reacted to pressure.”

“It feels that the administration is considering more about how do we respond to pressure rather than the kind of leadership, which should have been doing systemic work and prioritizing these issues all along,” she said.

Kotlikoff argued that replacing its leadership was not the solution.

“We need to be able to work together to be able to change the culture, educate our students and try and address this problem,” he said at the meeting. “I want Cornell to be a leader in this area, and we have plans to really invest in this area. But the idea that you can somehow, because an event has occurred, eliminate it immediately — it’s just unrealistic.”

Last month, a former student identified as Jane Doe sued the university and seven current and former students in connection with her allegation of sexual assault.

In 2024, Cornell shut down the Chi Phi fraternity chapter at the university and expelled two students after Doe reported the incident. Others were suspended or faced lesser disciplinary action. The university also said it launched the Presidential Task Force on Campus Sexual Assault shortly after the incident and implemented recommendations to address sexual assault on campus.

No criminal charges were brought at the time, and the investigation has been reopened following Jane Doe’s lawsuit. Four of the men, through their attorneys, have denied coercing Jane Doe with drugs or sexually assaulting her. NBC News was not able to reach the other three men named in the lawsuit.

While the faculty senate does not have the authority to remove the president, the move would greatly increase the pressure on Cornell and its administration.

Darlene Evans, a senior lecturer emerita, asked Kotlikoff why he was only taking steps now “towards serious systemic change” when he had been in leadership roles at the university for more than a decade.

Evans noted that more than 35% of female undergraduates surveyed at Cornell University reported experiencing nonconsensual sexual contact involving physical force, threats of force or incapacitation, according to a Cornell University poll conducted last year, a figure that was up from 23% in 2023.

“It wasn’t until a no-confidence vote was introduced that Cornell’s administration announced any real steps to prevent sexual assault on this campus, or to seriously support survivors,” she said. “So saying what we’re going to do now kind of rings hollow here. Why haven’t you taken these things more seriously until now, when there’s a firestorm of press looking at Cornell?”

Kotlikoff announced Tuesday that all parties at fraternity houses and events would be banned through the rest of the academic year.

“We don’t have full ability to be confident that what goes on in those houses is safe, and so for the time being we will stop that activity,” he said during the meeting Wednesday.

He also addressed calls from some over whether Greek life at the university should be banned altogether.

“If at the end of the day, fraternities cannot exist in a safe environment, and we can’t be convinced that they can be safe, then we should make that decision,” he said. “But we should make it based on data and study and expertise, not on emotion.”

After a question-and-answer session, the faculty senate began debating the no-confidence resolution, with another meeting scheduled for later this month. Many spoke in favor of the resolution, while others wanted to delay the vote until the results of an upcoming independent investigation.

Earlier this month, the university announced that Sally Yates, the former deputy U.S. attorney general and acting U.S. attorney general, would lead an independent review on how Cornell University responded to the allegations and, more broadly, how it responds to sexual harassment, assault and misconduct on campus.

New York Attorney General Letitia James is also investigating the allegation. A spokesperson said staff members from the attorney general’s office have “spoken with the Tompkins County District Attorney, Jane Doe’s attorney and several candidates for outside counsel to support the investigation.”

After the meeting, music professor Ariana Kim said she was “really inspired by everyone who spoke and was brave in favor of the resolution — it takes a lot to stand up in front of the president and ask direct questions of him.”

Kim said she has received some 200 emails from alumni saying they support the no-confidence resolution and want the administration to be held accountable.

The professor said some at the meeting held up signs that read, “I stand with Jane Doe,” “How many more?” and “We demand accountability.”

“Some people broke down and held each other after the meeting,” she said.

Political history professor Richard Bensel said that so far the central administration “has not responded in a way that is going to diminish faculty and students’ despair over the way that the university has treated the issue.”

Bensel said he was unsure if he wanted the president to resign, but said he thought university leadership “will not reform itself without passage of the no-confidence resolution.”

“I can imagine a way the trustees through the president can reconcile their relations with the Cornell community but that requires a real change in governance style, and I don’t think that is possible under this administration,” he said. “There are real problems in the way the university is run.”

World.title: Cracks are beginning to show in the stock market as doubts about AI investments grow
World.content:
Just one week after hitting fresh all-time highs, U.S. stocks are showing signs of strain as investors begin to fret about returns on the trillions of dollars that have been put into AI.

For U.S. consumers, it could mean a shakier economy moving forward.

After trading closed Thursday, the S&P 500 was off 1% from its week-ago record, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq had fallen more than 3% below its peak last week.

Driving the declines: Quarterly revenue growth at Anthropic has slowed, the Financial Times reported Wednesday. The AI giant is expected to be worth more than $1 trillion when it goes public, and at nearly $17 billion, its revenue is still massive and the company said it is profitable.

There are also rising concerns about whether China-based memory technology companies could undermine, or even overtake, their Western rivals. And even though the AI data center buildout has created a global shortage of processing chips, there are fears that Chinese mass production of memory chips could flood the market with an oversupply.

Meanwhile, investors have begun selling off the bonds backing some data centers, primarily over fears that AI revenues won’t be sufficient to cover the massive sums that have been borrowed to finance the building of the centers.

On Thursday, economist Ed Yardeni, a widely respected market commentator, lowered his year-end target for the S&P 500 to 7,900, down from 8,400, over what he said was rising investor caution about the artificial intelligence trade and lingering doubts about inflation and higher interest rates. The S&P 500 currently sits at about 7,600.

Most Americans don’t directly own tech stocks, let alone work in AI, which a growing number of studies show may have begun to limit job opportunities. Still, the AI buildout has been a massive part of what’s bolstering the economy, at least on paper.

Nearly half of all U.S. economy growth this year is attributable to tech-related spending. Those investments have also lifted the stock market even as a growing swath of other companies have experienced sharp declines in their share prices.

The tech-driven gains have in turn created a wealth effect that has helped propel steady U.S. consumer spending and, by extension, the job market. The result has been sturdy economic growth, even as lower-income and even middle-income households have continued to struggle under stubborn inflation and declining earnings.

“While higher interest rates, higher oil prices and persistent inflation create risks to the economy, strong positive forces such as the investment in AI infrastructure, high employment levels and consistent wage growth continue to outweigh the risks,” Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf said this week.

But other economists say consumers are already contending with a host of stressors that stand to weaken their position. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Thursday that inflation among businesses reached its highest rate since December 2022 — price growth that could eventually trickle down to consumers.

If tech spending — and stocks — show any sign of sustained declines, broader U.S. economic growth would likely be at risk.

“Higher interest rates, elevated energy prices, slow job growth and the sell-off in equities (if it continues) are all downside risks to consumer spending,” analysts with Citi wrote in a note Thursday.

World.title: Justice Dept. sues California, claims noncitizens were sent ballots
World.content:
Washington — The Justice Department sued California on Thursday, alleging that the federal government has identified more than 20,000 noncitizens who are unlawfully registered to vote.

The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, came after Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter sent letters to counties earlier this week, including Los Angeles, ordering them to review a list of names of suspected noncitizens who he alleged received mail-in ballots for the upcoming midterm elections.

"State-facilitated voter fraud is unacceptable in the United States of America," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement announcing the lawsuit.

"If found responsible in a court of law, the State of California will have seriously undermined confidence in our electoral system and violated laws that protect our nation's representative system of government."

In the letter that McCotter sent to the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk, he enclosed a password-protected thumb drive that he said contained names compiled by the Department of Homeland Security, and imposed a 48-hour deadline for the clerk's office to review the list.

Dean Logan, the registrar-recorder and clerk, said in a statement responding to McCotter's demands that the county would not be reviewing the materials on the thumb drive because doing so would conflict with "established data privacy and information security protocols." He said the device was not considered a "secure medium."

Secretary of State Shirley Weber, meanwhile, said the Justice Department had not provided the list of names and blasted the Trump administration for what it said were "unsubstantiated claims" that California had 190,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls.

In Thursday's lawsuit, the Justice Department accused the state of failing to work with the federal government to correct the alleged problems with its voter rolls.

"The Federal Government asked California to work collaboratively to identify any noncitizens registered to vote in the State. California made no serious effort to do so," the lawsuit said.

"The United States thus seeks commonplace election relief when a ballot is called into question. This Court should enjoin California from presently tabulating vote-by-mail ballots from likely noncitizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter's citizenship status can be determined," it added.

In a statement provided to CBS News, the California Secretary of State's office said, "Due to the pending litigation, we have no further information we can share regarding the matter." It directed CBS News to its news release on the situation and Weber's letter to McCotter.

CBS News has also reached out to the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk for comment.

The Justice Department's Civil Rights Division has filed 31 lawsuits in an effort to force states to hand over unredacted copies of their voter rolls. The division has said it wants to ensure states are keeping clean voter lists, but it has since acknowledged that it also intends to share the data with the Department of Homeland Security so that the lists can be screened for noncitizens.

Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general for the Civil Rights Division, sent letters to all 50 states in July threatening to take criminal action if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their voter rolls.

So far, the Justice Department has lost 26 of those cases, and has not achieved one legal victory to date.

It has resorted to using publicly available voter lists and other investigative means to try to identify noncitizens who may be registered in those states.

World.title: Soaring heating oil prices put struggling Maine families in a bind
World.content:
In Freeport, Maine, Chris and Cheryl Oliver are making tough choices as they try to make ends meet on roughly $60,000 a year.

"Am I going to get food this week, or am I going to get gas this week?" Cheryl Oliver told CBS News.

Then came another blow. Just as diesel and gas prices have risen considerably since the start of the Iran war, the price of heating oil in Maine has soared from $3.34 per gallon one year ago to $5.97 today, a jump of roughly 79%.



The Olivers qualified for 100 gallons of free heating oil through a local community center, help worth about $700. Unfortunately, it still won't get them through the winter.

"I was panicking, like, how are we going to fill our tank and how are we going to stay warm?" Cheryl Oliver asked.

Nationwide, more than 4 million households use heating oil as their primary fuel source, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, and of those, 82% are concentrated in the Northeast.

Tony DiMarco, co-founder of the Freeport Wood Bank, a food pantry of sorts for firewood, said the demand right now is "extremely high." Donations keep it running.



"I don't think people fully recognize how big of an impact it's going to have when heating oil costs twice as much as it did last year, and people are already spending as much as they did last year," DiMarco said. "I just don't think people fully grasp the severity of the problem."

The Freeport Wood Bank is one of about 17 similar wood banks across the state. Freeport can supply about 50 families with firewood, but DiMarco says it will run out of its supply by the middle of winter.

This week, DiMarco delivered two free cords of firewood to help the Olivers stretch their heating oil. It's a lifeline for a family already struggling. Chris Oliver lost one of his legs to diabetes and later suffered a heart attack.

"Tony and that place, they're unbelievable," an emotional Chris Oliver said. "I don't know without them if we'd have heat."

World.title: Maine couple forced to choose food or heat as oil prices skyrocket
World.content: Heating oil prices skyrocket in Maine Along with diesel and gas, the price of heating oil is up, and no state depends on it more than Maine. Meg Oliver spoke with residents there, now forced to make some tough decisions. More

World.title: Vance says "selling access to the White House" is "disgusting"
World.content:
Vice President JD Vance told CBS News on Thursday that anybody who is "selling access to the White House" should "suffer consequences."

Vance spoke with "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil during a one-hour town hall in Michigan that is set to air on Saturday evening, less than three weeks before the midterm elections.

Dokoupil pointed to a string of recent reports, including Mr. Trump's staggering cryptocurrency earnings, and the ousting of U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle over allegations she asked a man who was seeking help from the Trump administration to wire her $100,000.

"First of all, if somebody's selling access to the White House, that's disgusting and despicable and they should suffer consequences," Vance responded.

He went on to say, "I want to make those judgments based on the facts and not based on a random news media report that I read."

Guilfoyle has denied wrongdoing. Mr. Trump has denied any conflicts of interest.

Congressional Democrats have vowed to investigate the Trump administration if they win control of the House or Senate, which would grant them control over committees and allow them to issue subpoenas to administration officials.

Asked if the administration would comply with any subpoenas, Vance said: "Of course I will. Look, I mean, we follow the law."

Watch CBS News' "Things That Matter: A Town Hall With Vice President JD Vance" on Saturday, Oct. 17 at 8 p.m. ET/PT on the CBS Television Network or stream it on Paramount+. The one-hour special will also be available to watch afterward on CBSNews.com, YouTube and CBS News 24/7.
