World.title: 'Investors freaking out' about Wall Street big tech as warning bell rings
World.content:
The cost of insuring against a big technology firm defaulting on its debt has soared to record highs.

They are known as credit default swaps.

Heavily indebted data centre operator CoreWeave has been among the hardest hit.

Investors who have lent the company money are now paying a lot to buy these credit default swaps to insure against the risk of losing their investments if the company defaults.

The so-called neocloud company has taken on more than $US50 billion ($72 billion) in debt.

The yield on CoreWeave bonds set to mature in 2031 has hit 15.78 per cent.

This week, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps soared 16 per cent to a record 1.14 per cent, before easing slightly to 1.03 per cent.

Floodlines Research founder Anna Wu said the record highs in tech credit default swaps were an extension of CoreWeave's spreads blowing past 1 per cent.

"[It] has revived worries about how the AI build-out is being financed," Ms Wu said.

Turning to private credit

Wall Street's big tech firms are increasing turning to debt and private credit financing, having exhausted options to raise money in the share market.

But elevated global inflation is putting upwards pressure on interest rates, which is increasing the cost of this debt.

Competition for debt from governments and other big tech firms is also increasing interest rates, and the cost of servicing this debt.

Investors are growing increasing concerned the cost of the debt is growing too much for the big tech firms to service, and they are taking out insurance to prevent harmful financial loss.

Ms Wu conceded financial markets were growing more anxious about the financial health of these mammoth companies.

"Nvidia's Jensen Huang defended CoreWeave in Stockholm yesterday, saying its cost of capital is falling and it needs no Nvidia backstop, but I think investor sentiment on tech is fragile after the chip sell-off, so this is more sentiment than fundamentals for now," she said.

Elsewhere in the market cloud ⁠computing giant Oracle has seen its credit default swaps rise 0.3 per cent this week, while costs to insure against debt defaults for Nvidia, STMicroelectronics and SpaceX also rose sharply.

Credit default swap ⁠spreads for Amazon, Alphabet and Meta also traded at record highs, data from LSEG and S&P Global Market Intelligence showed, though they have risen far more slowly than Oracle, or CoreWeave.

Jensen Huang has defended CoreWeave's debt levels, saying its cost of capital is falling. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

"This is not the first time we've had a sizeable market wobble on the back of AI fears, ⁠but as we move to a capex cycle funded out of debt rather than simply free cash flow, we have to increasingly respect the credit price action," Deutsche Bank strategist Jim Reid said.

"AI financing costs aren't dramatic overall, but there are worrying themes at the edges."

Canary in the coalmine

Marcus Today senior markets analyst Henry Jennings described CoreWeave as the "canary in the coalmine" for excessive Wall Street big tech debt.

Wall Street risk signal flashing red Credit default swaps for US big tech companies are soaring to record highs. It means investors are fearful of a major Wall Street company collapse.

"[CoreWeave's credit default swaps show there is a] 60 per cent chance of default within five years," Mr Jennings said.

"Jensen Huang was quick to defend CoreWeave but then again, he is an investor and supplier to the company.

"Investors are freaking out on the cost of debt for wannabes," he said.

XTB research director Kathleen Brooks agreed.

"Its bonds have sold off sharply … this is a sign that investors might be going off the AI investment narrative, which has included massive debt issuance to fund AI ambitions."

ABC/Reuters

World.title: Safety concern in remote community with police station unstaffed
World.content:
A remote Far North Queensland community fears it is being left without police support while authorities try to fill vacancies at its empty police station.

Earlier this week, Queensland Police Service (QPS) confirmed the Laura police station was sitting empty while recruitment was underway to replace the solo officer, who had taken unplanned leave.

The remote Cape York township posting, 310 kilometres north-west of Cairns, covers a vast remote area incorporating the tourist gateway Peninsula Development Road (PDR).

QPS said patrols and call-outs in the meantime were covered by officers from Cooktown and Hope Vale, more than 140km away.

The Laura police district covers a large area in southern Cape York Peninsula. (ABC News: Peter Mullins)

The Indigenous Family Violence Legal Service said any gap in remote police staffing was deeply concerning for domestic violence victim-survivors.

Acting chief executive Thelma Schwartz said she was not surprised by the vacancy, describing remote understaffing as a long-standing problem.

"It doesn't matter if you're a victim-survivor of domestic, family and sexual violence living in metropolitan Queensland, regional Queensland, rural and remote Queensland," she said.

" The response from police should be the same: it should be urgent, it should be available. "

Thelma Schwartz is concerned an empty Laura police station puts women's safety at risk. (ABC News)

Ms Schwartz said she had frequently raised slow response times, including to the commission of inquiry into police domestic violence responses.

She said calls from towns without a local officer were diverted elsewhere, which could mean delays of several hours.

That risk grows as the wet season arrives and flooding threatens to cut roads across the tropical north.

Ms Schwartz said the risk of opportunistic violence from perpetrators due to lack of police presence was also well known.

Already underpoliced

Locals said the Laura division was already stretched even before the vacancy, with its two-officer posting long staffed by just one.

Palmerville Station resident Archie Levers said his community often had incidents where they struggled to get police support.

"We have a lot of illegal campers and illegal prospectors and people lighting fires, arsonists," he said.

" We had one incident last year that we had to call Mareeba police because we knew that it was serious. "

Laura is a remote centre in southern Cape York Peninsula. (Richard Dinnen)

Laura Quinkan Dance Festival organiser Debbie Symonds said she was concerned the community was not informed of the unstaffed police station, particularly given the amount of tourists passing through the area.

"It is the last bit of bitumen till they finish between the PDR before you hit dirt, and that's where a lot of issues can start and end in that town," she said.

While she welcomed news police were in the process of recruiting, she hoped QPS would ensure any new officers brought to the region were equipped to understand and work with the community.

"[We need] someone that is very balanced between cultural significance and events as well as being able to uphold law and be respected for that," she said.

Union critical of slow response

Queensland Police Union president Shane Prior said QPS could have sent a relief officer to Laura straight away while it recruited.

Laura is home to the famous Laura Quinkan Dance Festival. (ABC Far North: Christopher Testa)

"That position could have been filled, it simply wasn't because it was going to cost too much money," Mr Prior said.

" It's simply not good enough. The community of Laura deserved better. They deserve a police officer. "

Mr Prior said Laura was not an isolated case, with 745 positions vacant across the service.

Shane Prior has accused the police service of cost-cutting. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

He said the union met with QPS on Thursday morning and understood the station would be staffed as soon as possible.

A QPS spokesperson said recruitment for a relieving officer was underway, with the aim of having them start as soon as possible.

QPS said it could not detail how long Laura was unstaffed due to operational security.

"Far North police remain focused on the safety of local communities, their officers, and ensuring the highest levels of service delivery are always maintained," the QPS spokesperson said.

In a statement, Police Minister Dan Purdie said 272 new officers had been posted to the Far North since the LNP came to power.

World.title: House where Sydney couple died visited by Lamarre-Condon jury
World.content:
Jurors in the double murder trial of Beau Lamarre-Condon have visited the Sydney home where the former police officer is alleged to have shot Jesse Baird and Luke Davies.

The 15 jurors arrived at the terrace on Brown Street, Paddington, shortly after 10:30am on Friday after travelling by bus from the King Street Courthouse.

Family and domestic violence support services: NSW Domestic Violence Line on 1800 656 463

Lifeline on 131 114

Men's Referral Service on 1300 766 491

Mensline on 1300 789 978

Full Stop Australia on 1800 385 578

Emergency services on Triple Zero (000) if you need immediate care

Part of the street was closed off for the jury view.

Jurors were joined by the judge, Justice Natalie Adams, the prosecution team, including Crown Prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC, and Mr Lamarre-Condon's lawyers, including defence barrister John Stratton SC.

A witness who had previously given evidence about what police found in the terrace soon after the alleged murders, Senior Sergeant Bronwyn Lansley, was also present. Mr Lamarre-Condon did not attend.

The 31-year-old has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one of aggravated break and enter. His lawyers will argue self-defence.

The jury members are visiting the house to for "perspective and context". (ABC News: Simon Amery)

He is alleged to have used his police pistol to shoot Mr Baird, a television presenter, and Mr Davies, Mr Baird's new boyfriend and a Qantas flight attendant, on February 19, 2024, after Mr Baird's two housemates had left for work.

Senior Sergeant Lansley, a specialist crime scene officer, has previously given evidence at the trial, during which, the court was shown a floor plan of the property and dozens of photographs from inside.

Beau Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to two charges of murder. (Supplied: Liam Mendes)

Why scene visit is taking place

Ahead of the view, Justice Adams told the jury that the point of the visit was about "perspective and context".

"It's not always the same seeing it in the photograph, as seeing the actual premises," she said on Thursday afternoon.

Police tape outside the house in 2024. (Supplied)

Jurors have this week seen a 3D reconstruction video of the property showing the potential angles from which the gun could have been fired, according to evidence given by a ballistics expert from NSW Police.

The crime scene photographs shown to jurors included a fired cartridge case found on top of a kitchen cabinet, damage to a wall in the same room, and damage consistent with a bullet hole on the floor.

In a sub-floor area under the kitchen, police recovered a bullet.

Jesse Baird, left, and Luke Davies, right, died at the Paddington home. (Instagram)

Investigators belatedly discovered another hole in the door of the ground-floor bedroom in July this year, which had previously been covered by a stick-on hook.

The Crown's case is that Mr Lamarre-Condon developed an obsessive and jealous infatuation with Mr Baird after the two were romantically involved from 2022 into parts of 2023, a relationship Mr Baird considered casual.

Floor plan of Jesse Baird's home. (Supplied)

Mr Baird ended the relationship in November 2023 after discovering Mr Lamarre-Condon had interfered with his phone by blocking contacts, and had posted an Instagram story falsely suggesting he had sent Mr Lamarre-Condon flowers while in Melbourne.

Beau Lamarre-Condon's messages about Jesse Baird Texts between double-murder accused Beau Lamarre-Condon and a colleague show how he perceived his on-again-off-again relationship with alleged victim Jesse Baird.

The Crown alleges the accused dressed as an Uber Eats delivery driver and was wearing a helmet as he entered the Brown Street share house and shot Mr Baird twice in the kitchen, describing the second shot as an "execution-style" shot which went through the floor.

The prosecutor previously told jurors Mr Davies attempted to call Triple Zero (000) from the bedroom, and he was allegedly shot through the door by Mr Lamarre-Condon to eliminate a witness to Mr Baird's alleged murder.

Mr Lamarre-Condon's defence lawyers have indicated their case will be that Mr Baird and Mr Davies died during two separate struggles with the pistol.

Loading...

They argue that he panicked afterwards and cleaned the home because he knew how the situation would be perceived.

Multiple areas of blood staining in the home were documented, tested, and confirmed via DNA results to be that of Mr Baird and Mr Davies.

Forensic evidence gathered from the scene

The Crown alleges Mr Lamarre-Condon cleaned the property after the shootings and his housemates did not realise anything was amiss, a chemical called luminol was used to show a blue glow indicating the possible presence of blood on the floor, including large areas in the bedroom.

Under the floor, bloodstaining was discovered on timber beams and on the ground beneath the kitchen and bedroom, after police looked in the sub-floor area.

Mr Baird's two housemates, who were expecting him to move out that week, have recalled seeing two surfboard bags left in the courtyard with a red liquid underneath, which one housemate suspected was rusted water.

It is alleged Mr Lamarre-Condon stored the men's bodies in those bags before returning later to move them using a hired van.

The jury has previously been shown damage to the wall inside the home. (Supplied: NSW Supreme Court)

The bodies were ultimately found near a monastery in rural Bungonia, south of Sydney, eight days after the deaths.

Mr Lamarre-Condon is alleged to have unsuccessfully attempted to sink the bodies in a dam at a farm in the area using cement and weights, before returning to relocate them.

The jury has heard he had previously been to that property, which was owned by the family of a man he met on a dating app, in November 2023 after being invited for a weekend away.

The view of the Brown Street terrace marks the end of the fourth week of the trial, which has an estimated duration of three months.

World.title: Cowan handed AFL suspension following illicit substance investigation
World.content:
The AFL has suspended Carlton's Lachie Cowan for two matches following an investigation into his use of an illicit substance last weekend.

The league said "the circumstances in which the matter subsequently became public" were also the subject of the investigation.

Cowan was found guilty of conduct unbecoming.

He will be suspended for the first two home-and-away matches of the 2027 season and issued with a $5,000 fine.

Two Carlton AFL players hospitalised in Melbourne The club has confirmed Lachie Cowan and Will Hayward have been admitted to hospital under separate circumstances.

"I should never have put myself in such a vulnerable situation," Cowan said in a Carlton statement.

"I want to apologise for the impact my actions have had on my family and the football club.

"I also want to thank the medical professionals who helped me on the night, the football club for their ongoing support and everyone who took the time to reach out and make sure I was okay.

"This is a wake-up call and I am just so grateful to now be in a position to learn from this."

The Blues said Cowan's wellbeing remained a priority.

"Most importantly we are thankful that Lachie is okay and received the medical attention he needed," Carlton general manager of football Chris Davies said.

"We have been in regular contact with Lachie this week and he has taken ownership of his mistake.

"Lachie understands that it is his responsibility to ensure he makes better decisions moving forward."

Lachie Cowan issued an apology via the Carlton Football Club. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Michael Willson)

Cowan will be required to undertake further education above the current mandated training on illicit substances and their effects.

The league said the matter would "constitute a notifiable adverse finding under the AFL's illicit drugs policy".

"AFL players have a responsibility to themselves and their professional careers to uphold community expectations," AFL chief operating officer Tom Harley said in a league statement.

"They are well-educated when it comes to the harms associated with the use of illicit substances.

"Lachlan admitted his mistake and understands he must be accountable for his actions."

The AFL confirmed its new illicit drugs policy would come into effect in January.

The league said all players would be hair tested upon their return to training in January, "with readings going as far back as three to six months prior".

World.title: Mayor says flood-prone airstrip may need to move despite $27m upgrade
World.content:
A flood-prone airstrip in the Gulf of Carpentaria may need to be relocated to avoid future disasters, despite a recent multi-million-dollar upgrade, the local mayor says.

The community of Burketown, 420 kilometres north of Mount Isa, had been without a commercially functioning airstrip after a "biblical-style flood" engulfed the region in 2023.

For the past nine months while construction was underway, the only way in or out of the region has been by bus on unreliable dirt roads.

The Burketown airstrip upgrades after major flooding in 2023 cost $27 million. (Supplied: Durack Civil, Jake Rich)

The $27 million Queensland and federal government-funded upgrade raised the airstrip by 400 millimetres, and commercial flights are expected to resume in mid-November.

Burke Shire Mayor Ernie Camp said while it was positive to see the upgraded airstrip, owned and operated by the council, back up and running, it should be moved to a more flood-resistant location.

"[Regular Public Transport] services are the lifeblood for small communities, aircraft aren't getting any smaller, and the number of people travelling on them aren't either," he said.

Ernie Camp has been campaigning for regions in the Gulf of Carpentaria to be more flood-resilient. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

Although use of larger aircraft on Gulf routes could take years, he said planning ahead was key.

Cr Camp said he was a "little bit worried" the new airstrip would not survive another weather event like in 2023, but it was an improvement.

"It certainly has been an eye-opener in the amount of human resources and heavy equipment to come here because we had to totally rebuild that airstrip," he said.

"The tarmac had been compromised from not only the 2023 flood, [but also] the previous flood; the clay has certainly degraded."

Cr Camp said he had raised concerns with some politicians, but their suggestion was to "work with what we've got".

'Longevity' needed for Gulf investment

Western Queensland Alliance of Councils (WQAC) Executive Director Greg Hoffman said while he was pleased to see the airstrip improved and reopened, the challenge in the Gulf was to ensure assets have longevity and were not severely impacted by further weather events.

"The biggest challenge we have these days is to build sufficient resilience to get ahead of the game, so we don't find ourselves in five, 10 years having to do it again," Mr Hoffman said.

"[WQAC] has been very … in our advocacy to the governments to say that there needs to be long-term plans that take into consideration these potential adverse impacts into the future."

Mr Hoffman said investing to improve asset resilience was essential.

"Particularly in the case of Burketown and Gulf communities, the importance of air services and airports," he said.

"In the context of the importance of aerodromes in flood-prone areas, [Cr Camp's] argument has got a lot of merit [but] sadly, it will probably require a disaster to prove the point that what's been done at the moment hasn't achieved the objective of being flood-proof."

The RFDS and emergency services are crucial in Burketown, especially during the summer wet season. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

The government launched a joint $119 million flood recovery package across northern and central Queensland after the 2023 monsoonal event.

A spokesperson for Queensland Emergency Management Minister Ann Leahy said the Burketown Airstrip was a crucial public asset for residents, and it was unclear whether the federal government's proposed disaster funding cuts would have delivered this project.

The spokesperson did not respond to questions about relocating the airstrip.

A spokesperson for the Federal Minister for Emergency Management Kristy McBain said decisions around the future location of the Burketown airstrip were for local council to consider.

"Under the [Disaster Recovery Funding Arrangements], states and territories are responsible for determining whether a disaster is eligible for funding, and what type and level of assistance to make available to support recovery," the spokesperson said.

The Burketown airstrip was being repaired for about nine months. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

World.title: Sandalwood industry left in limbo as WA government mulls new rules
World.content:
Sandalwood producers in Western Australia say a lack of communication over looming changes to rules governing their lucrative industry has left them in limbo.

The native wood, prized for its use in perfumes, cosmetics and incense around the world, can fetch as much as $25,000 a tonne on the open market.

Sandalwood is one of the state's oldest export industries, dating back to 1844, and now a major cash crop in the Eastern Goldfields and Wheatbelt. (Supplied: Battye Library)

Under the current Sandalwood order, in place since 2015, 2,500 tonnes of wild sandalwood can be harvested annually.

But with that order due to expire at the end of this year, producers say the government has not been clear enough on what will replace it.

Sandalwood harvesting is managed by the Forest Products Commission, but new plans will restructure it under the DBCA.

Chief amongst their concerns is a proposed shift in oversight from the Forest Products Commission, the state's dedicated forestry body, to the larger Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions (DBCA), which governs WA's national parks and conservation estate.

Harvesters facing uncertain future

Michael Matthiessen says many are confused about how the transition to the DBCA is going to work. (Supplied: Mike Mathieson)

Harvester Michael Matthiessen got into the industry after moving to Kalgoorlie-Boulder, 600km east of Perth, 20 years ago.

While in favour of harvest reduction and a greater focus on regeneration, he said the shift to DBCA oversight had not been fully explained, and it was putting the industry in danger.

"I definitely think there's a risk to the industry if the transition isn't managed properly," he said.

"No one has been asking the questions to myself or other contractors that would give our perspective on the industry.

"And what is and isn't important going forward."

With sandalwood trees taking upwards of two decades to mature, Mr Matthiessen said harvesters needed to plan years in advance, making uncertainty challenging.

"It takes a lot of time, effort, resources and experience to be a really efficient and effective harvesting contractor," he said.

"Once it's gone, it's going to be quite difficult to recover."

Native sandalwood chips thrive in tough, arid environments. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

The ABC asked WA Premier Roger Cook about the industry's concerns and he said the government were stepping through the process carefully.

"We're consulting widely and doing some work inside the FPC at the moment just to make sure we've got the best settings," he said.

Exporters warn of international impact

Exporters share the on-the-ground harvester's concerns.

Wescorp Sandalwood executive chair Fleur Coakley said the industry was being left in the dark.

"FPC contracts are coming up to finish at the end of December, and none of us knows what's happening beyond that," she said.

"If it's not managed well and there isn't that cycle of investment going in … that's what my customers internationally are already concerned about."

Sandalwood oil can sell for nearly $2,000 per 100ml. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Ms Coakley recently joined a number of industry stakeholders, backed by the state opposition, to call for greater transparency from the government.

"Everyone's not sure whether we invest or whether we start doing plan B," she said.

"There's really no clarity at all and no formal announcement for any of us."

Ms Coakley is worried that the lack of clarity is creating uncertainty among investors and is worried about the impacts on the international market.

She wants the state to take a greater focus on illegal harvesting and regeneration.

"We've had different views, different approaches, and there's no continuity of discussing how transitions will happen or how this might work," Ms Coakley said.

"Having those different government departments, different ministers, it's really confused all of us."

Sandalwood heartwood can sell for $15,000 a tonne, but the slow-growing plant is considered vulnerable in the wild. (ABC Goldfields: Andrew Chounding)

WA Forestry Minister Jackie Jarvis and Environment Minister Mathew Swinbourn were both contacted to comment on industry's concerns.

Neither minister responded; however, in a written statement, a state spokesperson said a draft review was available and being reviewed by an independent panel.

"The Cook government is committed to facilitating discussion between interested parties to collaborate on what a future sustainable wild sandalwood industry could look like," the statement said.

The FPC and DBCA declined to comment.

Alternate models

Not everyone in the industry shares these concerns; Kalgoorlie-Boulder-based oil producer Dutjahn is one of the state's largest oil producers.

Director Keith Drage argues the industry has had time to prepare.

"Everybody's been aware that the current order … expires at the end of 2026," he said.

"Obviously we have very much a vested interest in what happens between now and then and thereafter."

Keith Drage and Darren Farmer from Dutjahn Sandalwood Oils. (Supplied: Jody D'Arcy)

Mr Drage said a transition away from government harvest on crown land to a mixture of independent Aboriginal operators and plantation resources was an inevitable outcome.

"We've always seen … that that was going to eventuate," he said.

"A diminishing wild harvest in Aboriginal hands is something that we've always built our business model around."

World.title: Chickens allowed free range again in Victoria as bird flu lockdown ends
World.content:
A lockdown order to protect Victorian poultry farms from H5N1 bird flu is being lifted today, despite the continuing spread of the deadly disease among wildlife.

Flocks of 50 or more birds in metropolitan Melbourne and southern parts of the state have been forced to stay indoors, or be confined, since the order was first announced in early August.

H5N1 is spreading among wildlife in Australia but has not been detected in poultry or livestock.

The control order applied in Melbourne and across southern parts of Victoria. (Supplied: Agriculture Victoria)

Agriculture Victoria said it took into consideration "animal welfare" and "hotter than average" forecast summer temperatures when deciding to lift the housing order.

Chief veterinary officer Graeme Cooke said farmers were supportive of the protection measures so far.

He said producers needed to continue to protect their flocks from wildlife as much as possible.

"Reducing contact between poultry and wild birds remains one of the most effective ways to lower the risk of disease," he said.

" We strongly encourage poultry owners to continue taking practical steps to separate birds wherever possible. "

Graeme Cooke says poultry flocks should be protected from wild birds. (ABC Landline: Tim Lee)

Biosecurity 'best defence'

The lifting of the order brings 10 weeks of lockdown to an end for poultry farmers in Victoria's south.

"It's been a huge joint effort to keep bird flu out of our commercial poultry industry," Victorian Farmers Federation president Ryan Milgate said.

Ryan Milgate says farmers need to remain vigilant for any signs of bird flu. (ABC News: Sean Warren)

"Strong biosecurity practices remain our best defence to reducing the risk of disease outbreaks, such as H5."

Mr Milgate urged producers to stay on the lookout for sick or diseased birds.

"We must not rest on our laurels and become complacent," he said.

There have been 234 confirmed events of H5N1 in wildlife in Victoria so far.

And while the lockdown ends today, Dr Cooke says the risk of disease spread remains.

"We will continue monitoring the risk closely and retain the ability to introduce additional controls if circumstances change."

Victorians have been told to avoid contact with unwell or dead wildlife.

Reports can be made to the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline on 1800 675 888 or on the Agriculture Victoria website.

World.title: Live: Children among dead in shooting at elementary school in Oregon
World.content:
Authorities believe at least five people are dead following a shooting at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon.

Officials told the Associated Press on condition of anonymity that the death toll was preliminary and could change.

CNN and CBS News, citing law enforcement sources, reported that one adult and three children were killed in the violence, but it was not immediately clear whether the shooter was included in that death toll.

Live Moment Live updates, reactions and contributions from ABC readers. Shooter 'forced' his way into elementary school E Eden Regan The 16-year-old suspect gained entry into the school by shooting at locked doors. . From what the initial investigation is showing is that the shooter had forced their way into the school by shooting locked doors Bend City Police Chief Mike Krantz said he could not confirm how the suspect got into the school before he was gunned down Authorities unaware of shooter's potential connection to school Police and government officials in the room have been asked whether they know if the alleged shooter knew any of the students or staff at Silver Rail Elementary School. "Unfortunately, I'm unable to answer that at this point," Bend City Police Chief Mike Krantz says. "We just don't have that information yet." Investigation in early stages Given the early stages of the investigation, police couldn't comment on what kind of gun was used other than to say it was a long gun. They were also unable to disclose how many rounds were used. Governor confirms multi-agency response to shooting The Governor of Oregon, Tina Kotek, says "all Oregonians will mourn this loss". "This is a horrible day, no parent should have to have this kind of day," Ms Kotek says. The governor says the Oregon Department of Emergency Management is coordinating the official response to the shooting, including by communicating with multiple state agencies. Bend City Mayor planning community vigil Melanie Kebler, the mayor of Bend City, has now started to speak. She also describes the shooting today as "an awful day for our community". "A school should be a safe place where children can learn and feel secure. What happened today should never happen," she says. Ms Kebler says authorities will look to organise a community vigil in the coming days "to mourn together, honour those affected and those lost, and begin the difficult process of healing". "I extend my deepest condolences to every person impacted by this tragedy. We grieve with you, and we'll support one another through the difficult days ahead," she says. School superintendent 'heartbroken' by shooting Steve Cook, the superintendent of Bend-La Pine Schools which includes the Silver Rail Elementary School, is next to begin speaking. He appears quite sombre at the lectern, and is describing the shooting as "an unspeakable tragedy". "No community should have to do what we're doing right now," he says.

"I don't have any words for what the community is feeling. I don't think anyone does. "We are heartbroken, we are horrified, this is the kind of thing you hear about in other places and pray it never happens here, and it's happened here. "Today it happened to our children, to our teachers and to our families. "To the families that have had loss tonight, we're with you and we will stay with you. "To our staff who helped our students and protected our kids today, we thank you — you did what no one should ever be asked to do." Mr Cook says that all school activities have been cancelled for Friday, local time, and crisis counsellors are being made available for students, families, staff and others who need support. "Please hold your children, hold your loved ones tight together, let them talk, let them cry, let them know we're going to rally and care for one another in this community," he says. "We'll get through this." Three children among dead, chief says Officers arrived at the scene where they found three children, aged 5, 8 and 11, deceased, alongside one teacher. A 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher have been rushed to hospital in a critical condition, he said. Authorities say the investigation will be 'long' Mr Krantz said the investigation would be long after authorities identified the teen as a Bend resident. "These things take time, and we appreciate your patience," he said. "This is a terrible tragedy," Mr Krantz said Five people died from injuries during shooting Chief Krantz says officers entered the school and found the 16-year-old suspect dead. Mr Krantz confirmed a community member observed the teen enter the school and pursued him before shooting him dead. Police timeline of US school shooting incident Bend City Police Chief Mike Krantz is the first to begin speaking and is outlining the timeline of today's shooting. Chief Krantz says at 12:59pm, local time (5:59am AEST), county emergency dispatchers received a 911 call from a person in a vehicle who reported being shot at by someone armed with a long gun. He says dozens of other emergency calls were then made to authorities, including from people reporting the alleged shooter had entered a Silver Rail Elementary School building. At 1:01pm, the school was ordered into a lockdown, and a minute later the first police officers arrived on the scene. Moments after that, the suspected shooter "was shot by a community member who saw the suspect enter the school and pursued him and engaged him," Chief Krantz says.

"Our officers entered the building and confirmed the suspect was dead," Chief Krantz says. Show more

Both news outlets reported later that the shooter was 16 years old, with CNN describing the teen as a boy.

Bend Police Department communications manager Sheila Miller told reporters she had no information about the shooter, who was shot and killed.

A subsequent police statement, posted online, said authorities "have confirmed there were multiple victims", with at least two taken to hospital, adding, "children are among the victims".

Ms Miller told reporters investigators had yet to confirm who shot the suspect.

First responders at the scene following a shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon. (Reuters: Rob Kerr)

"We don't have confirmation yet of who shot the suspect; it may have been a bystander," Ms Miller said.

Authorities received a call about a shot fired into a car outside Silver Rail Elementary about 12:59pm, local time, and arrived on scene within minutes.

She said further 911 calls came from inside the school.

Police arrived on campus within minutes, and the shooter was shot almost immediately, Ms Miller said.

Silver Rail Elementary was under lockdown, the Bend-La Pine school district wrote on Facebook.

"We're in the process at this time of going room by room and evacuating each of the people who are in that school," Ms Miller said.

"This is the kind of thing we never want to see happen in Bend. It's devastating," she said, pausing to control her emotions.

Bend is a city of about 100,000 people in central Oregon, about 280 kilometres south-east of Portland.

Silver Rail Elementary School serves students from kindergarten through to fifth grade, aged from about five to 11.

It has about 450 students and 40 staff members, Ms Miller said.

FBI chief Kash Patel said on X that federal agents were also on the scene "assisting our local partners in the investigation".

"We will make every resource they need available," he said.

US Representative Maxine Dexter, a physician who represents a portion of Portland east of the Willamette River, called the shooting a "devastating day for Oregon".

"Schools should be places of learning, friendship and joy," she said.

"It is incumbent on me, and every lawmaker, to do everything we can to ensure our kids are safe," Ms Dexter said in a statement.

Governor Tina Kotek said separately on X: "As we learn more about the tragic event at Silver Rail Elementary in Bend today, we must come together and support each other, neighbor to neighbor, Oregonian to Oregonian. No community should have to live through this day."

Reuters/AP

World.title: Even Stephen Curry’s King Arthur can’t save stale Spamalot, plus other new shows this week
World.content:
Sydney Event Centre, October 15. Until October 18

There’s a scene early in Spamalot, where a man wanders the streets of a plague-ridden town in medieval England pushing a cart piled with lifeless bodies, shouting “Bring out your dead!” Lancelot enters dragging a body, which struggles out of his clutches crying “I am not dead yet”. Cue music for a jaunty song and dance number.

Stephen Curry plays King Arthur in Spamalot Ben Fon

“I’m not dead yet” is one of those classic Monty Python lines, greeted by laughs and cheers by a hyped-up fandom on the first night. But is there still life in the old thing? I’m not convinced.

Spamalot, subtitled “A new musical lovingly ripped off from the motion picture Monty Python and the Holy Grail”, was created by Monty Python original Eric Idle in 2006. It had a successful Broadway run, scooping up a fistful of Tony Awards. This Australian production, produced and directed by Drew Anthony, is a competent rehash starring Stephen ‘The Castle’ Curry as King Arthur and an enthusiastic all-singing, all-dancing ensemble.

Marney McQueen as the Lady of the Lake.

The plot is an undergrad rewrite of the Arthurian legend. God commands King Arthur to find the Holy Grail. Arthur recruits a motley posse of knights and, after a glow-up at Camelot, they grab their coconut shells (clip-clop, clip-clop) and set out. The quest takes them to France, where they meet flatulent locals, knights who say “Ni!”, and a Black Knight who is harder to kill than a cockroach. But do they find the grail?

Curry is not an obvious choice as lead but makes a good fist of the preening role of Arthur, despite his tortuous English accent. His sidekick Patsy, played by Jamie Rolton, who also choreographs the show, frequently upstages the king with his well-timed quips and genial stage presence. Marney ‘Titanique’ McQueen sings her heart out as Lady of the Lake, leaning into the diva energy of Whatever Happened To My Part?, while Gareth Isaac as Sir Robin bubbles with showtime glee while singing You Won’t Survive On Broadway Without Jews. Awkward.

Stephen Curry as King Arthur with the cast in a scene from Spamalot. Ben Fon

Drew Anthony’s design concept is a deliberate collision of low-fi production values and technological wizardry. The costumes are straight from the dress-up box, and dad made the props, while the backdrop (by Travis Badge of Aquixel) transports us to rolling hills and luxuriant forests, and even provides a fully digital cast member, the Black Knight, yelling “’tis but a flesh wound” as it spurts bloody pixels.

It’s not the cast’s fault that this show fails to dazzle: the gags are desperately dated and the music is derivative. That is not a guarantee of failure in itself – lots of musical theatre shows thrive on in-jokes and self-parody – but the many compromises, including canned music and a terrible venue, do nothing to lift the raw material out of its nostalgic soup. Without the bite of up-to-date satire and the zing of in-the-moment comic improv, Spamalot has no teeth. This one’s strictly for the fans.

Spamalot also shows at Coliseum Theatre, Rooty Hill from October 22-25.

Police have locked down part of Dulwich Hill in Sydney’s inner west after reports a man armed with a shotgun is in the area. Heavily armed tactical police, along with a police helicopter and general duties officers, rushed to the area near Williams Parade and Constitution Road about 10.30am on Friday, after gunshots were reported to emergency services. Police have shut down the area as they comb Dulwich Hill for the gunman. James Brickwood Police responded to reports of gunfire in Dulwich Hill on Friday. 9News Nearby businesses and cafés have been put into lockdown, along with Dulwich Hill Public School, as officers hunt the man who is allegedly armed with a sawn-off shotgun.



Witnesses on the ground told Nine News there had been an altercation between the man and another group of people, which ended in a car being set alight by an apartment complex. Tactical police, along with the police helicopter, are combing the suburb for the man. Nine News A Dulwich Hill café has been shut down, while locals have been asked to remain indoors. Nine News A large exclusion area has been established, as police search for the gunman. Locals have been urged to remain inside, while those travelling through Dulwich Hill have been redirected from the area. No injuries have been reported, nor have any arrests been made. Light rail services between Dulwich Hill and Lilyfield have been stopped amid the ongoing operation.



The operation comes after bullets were sprayed at a house in Sydney’s south-west at 12.35am on Friday, occupied by two men, 21 and 23, and a 59-year-old woman. Police responded to the house in Willis Street, Lansvale, before stopping a grey sedan at nearby Hollywood Drive. Officers allegedly found a balaclava and firearm in the car shortly after the drive-by shooting, before arresting its occupants – two males, 17 and 18, and a 17-year-old girl. The trio were arrested and taken to Cabramatta Police Station, where they faced police questioning. No charges have been laid. The occupants of the targeted house were uninjured. More to come

World.title: Principal admits ‘failures’ after anti-abortion speaker addressed Scotch students
World.content:
Breaking NationalVictoriaPrivate schools Principal admits ‘failures’ after anti-abortion speaker addressed Scotch students Caroline Schelle October 16, 2026 — 12:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The principal of one of the state’s most exclusive private schools has apologised after a controversial anti-abortion speaker addressed year 11 boys in a presentation that shocked students and staff. Dr Emma Wood spoke to the students in September as part of the school’s Christian education curriculum. Scotch College’s principal has apologised after a controversial anti-abortion speaker addressed year 11 boys. Wayne Taylor Wood runs the anti-abortion “Pro-Love Logic” organisation and gives presentations to help students understand the relationship between “widespread abortion and the individualistic sexual culture the West has embraced”. Principal Scott Marsh sent a letter to parents of year 11 students on Friday after he commissioned an internal review.



“I am ultimately responsible for activities involving our students,” Marsh wrote in the letter seen by The Age. He said the review found there were procedural failings in how the presentation was arranged and managed. “The presentation should have been classified and managed as an incursion because it involved an external speaker addressing boys outside the normal class timetable,” Marsh wrote. The principal said it was a clear failure in processes. “We are sorry for the distress this caused some boys and families,” he said.



Related Article Exclusive

Education Scotch College students and staff left reeling by anti-abortion activist’s lecture However, he did not apologise for the content of the speech delivered by Wood. Her presentations for high school students include defining abortion as “an act of harm inflicted on an unborn human being that both intends and accomplishes that unborn human’s death”. The all-boys school was established in 1851, and is the oldest secondary school in Victoria. Based in Hawthorn, it educates nearly 2000 boys from prep to year 12. From next year, it will charge more than $47,000 for year 11 students. The principal said in his letter that the review did not make any findings against individual staff members, but focused on what occurred, the procedural failings and how to address them.



“A further session will be held for the same year 11 cohort this term,” Marsh said. “It will present a different perspective on the topic and provide boys with a further opportunity to consider, discuss and reflect on the issues raised within their Christian education classes.” A source not authorised to speak publicly said Wood’s lecture had made staff and students feel uncomfortable. “Everyone was taken aback … it wasn’t a discussion,” they said. In a previous letter from the principal to parents in September, he said the controversial speaker was recommended by other schools.



It did not go into detail about which schools recommended Wood. Wood teaches at Campion College in NSW, which was investigated after its dean of studies and a senior history lecturer made comments supporting the White Australia policy. Wood, who holds a PhD in philosophy from Victoria University of Wellington and “specialises in bioethics and political philosophy”, according to her website, did not respond to multiple requests for comment. World.title: Climb this spiral staircase for the long lunch of your dreams
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

There’s the mood, attentive but casual and oh-so-warm, as though any worries you have can be allayed by simply shrugging off a coat. There’s the structure: a set menu (two courses early in the week, four on weekends) with few decisions required. Add oysters? Room for cheese? Where’s your thirst leaning? And there’s the food, of course. It’s all sourced locally, from growers known by name.

Up a spiral staircase, on the top floor of an 1858 building that was once the Daylesford grocer, there’s now a cosy dining room lined with artwork, arranged salon-style, on mustard-coloured walls. Stepping up the tight whorl is like spinning yourself into a fantasy: all your dining dreams are about to come true.

You can engage with this as much as you like: there’s no brittle culinary ego hovering and demanding you fall into silence with every lovely bite. Your informed waiter knows about the saucisson (perhaps crafted from Brooklands pork, a free-range farm in nearby Blampied) or the polenta (from corn harvested by Tumpinyeri Growers over yonder, milled on-site by co-head chefs Oliver Edwards and Bree Smith). But you can just keep sipping the wine (maybe the grenache from Dilworth and Allain, who have a cellar door around the corner) and sink into a reverie.

The menu changes weekly. That polenta might be the smooshy base for octopus

braised in red wine, or pork cooked in sage and milk, the latter from Tess Sellar, who runs a dairy herd of just 10 cows. It’s rustic stuff, made for eating, not Instagram. Even so, the salad gleams in its dressing, every leaf just so, and the roasted flathead flakes easily, as though a card sharp is dealing a royal flush, and the sweet cream squeezes lusciously from a crisp-crackled choux puff.

Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up

Roasted flathead, salad and potato bake. Bonnie Savage

Merenda turns five this month. Owners Andy and Clare Ainsworth are Sydney

escapees with backgrounds in hospitality and wine (him) and illustration (her). In 2020, they decided central Victoria was something of an antipodean Provence and built a life there, followed by a wine bar in Daylesford’s divey old pizza shop.

The first iteration of Merenda was beautiful and fun, though a little clunky, because there was no way to separate boisterous drinkers from special-occasion diners. The current space, inhabited a year ago, means diners are ensconced up those spiral stairs, while drop-ins are downstairs at the bar, where the food

is as good, just a little simpler. Maybe there’s duck: the grilled breast appears in the bistro with lentils and braised greens, while the legs are confited for the bar. Everyone wins.

World.title: December rare earths production debut looms for Lindian in Malawi
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears December rare earths production debut looms for Lindian in Malawi Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward October 16, 2026 — 12:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. ASX 300-listed Lindian Resources has the pedal to the metal at its Kangankunde rare earths project in Malawi, with construction hitting key milestones as it heads towards first monazite concentrate production in December. Kangankunde’s sheer scale has captured global attention, with the project considered one of Africa’s most significant rare earths deposits. It hosts a massive 261-million-tonne resource grading an impressive 2.19 per cent total rare earth oxides (TREO). Within that inventory is a high-grade core of 26 million tonnes at a hefty 3.7 per cent TREO, earmarked as the initial feed for the stage-one plant. Installation works completed across the Kangankunde process plant’s separation circuits ahead of commissioning at Lindian Resources’ Kangankunde rare earths project in Malawi, with first production targeted for December. The company says its construction and operational readiness activities are progressing on multiple fronts. Structural steel installation in the plant’s wet high-intensity magnetic separation and magnetic gravity separation areas is now 90 per cent complete. The installation of shaking tables is 80 per cent done, while the crucial regrind mill has been installed and piping is being laid. On the power front, the 33-kilovolt overhead transmission line has now been commissioned through to the transformer yard. Both of its 1250 kilovolt-ampere plant transformers have passed factory acceptance testing in Malawi and are back on site, ready to be fired up in the first week of November. Lindian says this will allow time for motor testing and electrical commissioning ahead of introducing the first ore to the plant.



‘Every milestone brings us closer to becoming a rare earths producer.’ Lindian Resources executive director Zac Komur While construction pushes ahead, mining operations have continued to swell run-of-mine (ROM) stockpiles. The company says it now has 149,000 tonnes of ore on the ROM pad, up 19 per cent from the 125,000 tonnes held in September. Mining has also moved to the pit’s upper levels, with drilling underway from the top of the hill to open up additional mining faces. Lindian executive director Zac Komur said: “Kangankunde is in the final stretch of construction. Our target is clear: first monazite concentrate in December. The plant is taking shape, ore stockpiles are growing and our focus is on completing the remaining work and commissioning safely. Every milestone brings us closer to becoming a rare earths producer.” Lindian’s push to become Africa’s next rare earths producer is playing out against a backdrop of intense global competition for the critical minerals. Rare earths have become a focal point of supply chain security, with the International Energy Agency warning that industries from automotive and defence to electronics face significant exposure to Chinese supply constraints. This has sparked a flurry of dealmaking, with rare earths accounting for more than nine per cent of global mining and metals transaction value in the first half of this year. Major financing and acquisitions have been seen in Australia, Brazil and the United States as the West tries to build out alternative supply chains.



Notably, stage one of the Kangankunde project is fully funded through to production, backed by a long-term strategic partnership and offtake deal with major mineral sands producer Iluka Resources. The project’s progress also appears to have the support of the Malawian government, which has a stated policy of encouraging in-country value-addition for its minerals before export. Importantly for the company’s social licence to operate, locals make up 85 per cent of Lindian’s direct workforce of 3000 people, overwhelmingly Malawian nationals, currently employed across the broader construction of the project. Lindian’s on-site concentrate production dovetails neatly with its broader downstream ambitions, having also acquired the SARECO mixed rare earth carbonate processing facility in Kazakhstan to capture more value from its Malawian product. The company has also locked in a partnership with French processing expert Carester to develop an oxide separation facility in Kazakhstan, along with a binding offtake agreement for its future high-value heavy rare earth products. This, combined with its portfolio of bauxite assets in Guinea and Tanzania, positions the company as an increasingly diversified international player with operations spanning multiple commodities and jurisdictions.



With the plant taking shape and power about to flow, Lindian is almost set for the transition to full-time operations. The first plant supervisor and two control room operators are on the books and operator training has begun. Key consumables have been secured and outbound logistics contracts covering rail transport and freight forwarding are now being finalised for execution ahead of the first shipment. As the clock ticks down to its December production target, Lindian appears to be in the box seat and speeding towards delivering a new, large-scale source of rare earths into a market that is crying out for supply chain diversity. World.title: Ukraine’s latest battlefield drone is about to enter the kill zone – to fly out the wounded
World.content:
WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war Ukraine’s latest battlefield drone is about to enter the kill zone – to fly out the wounded Samya Kullab October 16, 2026 — 11:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A secret location in Ukraine: Six propellers whir to life, lifting a drone above a field. A weighted stretcher secured to its frame simulates a wounded soldier in body armour. Far from the front line, the demonstration offers a glimpse of a far more dangerous mission: flying into a battlefield where enemy drones and artillery can leave wounded troops stranded for weeks or months, then carrying them to safety without an evacuation crew. Loading Some of the more harrowing footage to emerge from this war has been drone tracking and striking fallen soldiers with nowhere to flee. AP was granted exclusive access to a field demonstration of the drone. This week, StarGate was handed over to a combat brigade for evaluation under front-line conditions.



The aerial medical evacuation drone was developed over the past year by Ukrainian defence technology company SkyFall. If it proves reliable in combat, it could transform battlefield evacuations, reaching soldiers in places that ground vehicles cannot access and potentially saving those so severely wounded that hours of waiting could cost them their lives. “The idea came directly from the front line, from the trenches,” said SkyFall’s spokesperson, who asked not to be named because of the security risks facing Ukrainian military technology personnel. He spoke wearing a balaclava and AP was not permitted to disclose the testing location. The Associated Press was granted exclusive access to the StarGate demonstration. AP In some sectors, the so-called kill zone – the area under constant threat from drones and artillery – stretches 10 to 15 kilometres or further. StarGate has a one-way range of 15 kilometres, potentially allowing it to reach critically wounded soldiers trapped deep inside the kill zone. A request from a military commander



The idea grew out of a military request, the spokesperson said. Last year, “Flint”, commander of the 475th Separate Assault Regiment known as Code 9.2, approached SkyFall’s founder about developing a safer way to evacuate wounded soldiers from hard-to-reach positions. For troops in Code 9.2, reaching a front-line position to retrieve the wounded can mean travelling on foot through areas where vehicles are vulnerable to drones. Unmanned ground vehicles have taken on a growing role in evacuating casualties and delivering supplies, but they struggle through mud, craters and shattered roads. Rivers, mines and drones can stop them altogether. A drone pilot operates the new StarGate at an undisclosed location in Ukraine. AP Ground robots typically take two to three hours to reach a position, depending on distance, road conditions and the threat from above, said “KVN”, a commander with Code 9.2. “Covering 10 kilometres in minutes would be a drastic change on the front line,” he said.



Evacuations continue regularly in his unit’s area, he said, but it is not always possible to retrieve a wounded soldier on the same day. For someone with severe injuries, the wait can be critical. Both Flint and KVN were identified only by their call signs in line with Ukrainian military protocol. The StarGate drone, equipped with a medical module, deploys a net designed to intercept aerial threats. AP SkyFall emerged after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, and has grown into a Ukrainian drone manufacturer. Its Vampire heavy-lift drone, known to Russian forces as “Baba Yaga”, is used by Ukrainian troops for battlefield missions. The company also makes Shrike, a first-person-view drone, and has developed the P1-SUN aerial interceptor. Named after the science-fiction franchise in which portals connect distant worlds, StarGate can carry a payload of up to 150 kilograms, according to the company – enough for a wounded soldier wearing body armour and carrying combat equipment. Its medical evacuation cabin is built around a stretcher.



The drone cruises at 65km/h and can reach speeds of up to 105km/h. SkyFall says it can be prepared for flight in about 10 minutes. Duelling drone tests At the test field, StarGate lifts off as first-person-view drones buzz towards it, simulating the aerial threats that dominate Ukraine’s front line. Electronic jamming is activated. As one attacking drone closes in, a net shoots out, ensnaring it and sending it off course. Military medics treat a wounded Ukrainian soldier in the field hospital in the Zaporizhzhia region, Ukraine, last month. Ukrainian 65 Mechanised Brigade/AP The encounter resembles a futuristic duel fought by machines. But carrying a wounded soldier raises the stakes.



One of SkyFall’s biggest challenges was ensuring the drone could navigate when electronic warfare disrupts communications or interferes with GPS signals. StarGate uses two communication channels – Starlink and the company’s proprietary L-Link system – alongside an artificial intelligence-based system to help it maintain control when satellite navigation is unavailable. The drone is operated manually, but has several AI functions that allow it to operate in GPS-denied environments or when signals are spoofed or frequencies are jammed, the spokesperson said. A Ukrainian serviceman launches a drone towards Russian positions at the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region last week. Ukrainian 65 Mechanised brigade/AP If communication is lost entirely, SkyFall says, the drone can plot a route back to a safe area. It is designed to operate in rain and snow, with thermal-imaging cameras for nighttime missions. SkyFall also says it has demonstrated the drone’s ability to continue flying after losing one of its arms. The company has not provided data showing how reliably it can withstand damage under combat conditions. The drone began front-line tests this week.



From prototype to combat ready drone Related Article Updated

Russia-Ukraine war ‘Betrayed’: Ukraine leader denounces Trump for siding with Russia amid row with Musk StarGate has undergone multiple design changes, including detachable arms for easier transport, a medical-grade stretcher and improved software and defences. The company estimates each system will cost at least $US50,000 ($72,000), depending on configuration, and aims to produce up to 1000 a month by the end of 2026. For KVN, however, it is too early to judge. His unit needs at least a month of experience with the drone before it can provide meaningful statistics on its success rate.



“It’s a completely new method of evacuation,” he said. “It’s difficult to talk in depth about the pros and cons right now. We need to work with it more.” SkyFall confirmed the unit was evaluating StarGate but declined to disclose the results. World.title: What my father Bruce taught me, and why I’ll always stare at fish
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsHistory Opinion What my father Bruce taught me, and why I’ll always stare at fish Julia Baird Journalist, broadcaster, historian and author October 16, 2026 — 11:54am

October 16, 2026 — 11:54am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Last week I returned to the University of Sydney to accept an honorary doctorate. It was wonderful to be back at a place that shaped my life and the lives of my family; where I’d spent the best part of a decade studying arts, and some law, and then diving into history to write a PhD that took a ridiculously long time and caused clumps of my hair to fall out. History, like careers, like human lives, never operates in a straight line. It gets knocked out of shape by events, like all of us, like the human heart. Julia Baird speaks to graduates at the University of Sydney earlier this month. Franky Tsang On that day my heart was particularly dented because that place was also where my father, alongside my mother, studied arts in the ’60s. He went on to live a big life of public service, humanity and adventure. He died suddenly, before I was due to speak at the university, and I thought about not going. But I was there because he would have wanted me there, along with my family – mainly because he loved attention and fancy hats and would have been horrified at the prospect of my forgoing either on his account. Dad always said Mum was the great scholar, not him. Which may be fair. But he was a great human. And he paid attention, especially to the things that aren’t written down, that aren’t on the syllabus. He paid attention to people, and to the ocean.



He taught me to push forward in the surf, to enter the ocean every day no matter your mood or workload, no matter the colour of the skies, the size of the waves (within reason), to dive in and just try, to give it a crack. When you find people who believe in you, don’t take them for granted. Keep them by your side. Julia Baird and her father, Bruce Baird, in the ocean. I’ve worked most of my life as a journalist but history is the first great love of my life. History has sneaked me into the best places, like a friend who knows the bouncer (hang on to those people, too, by the way). History has taken me to secret archives in Windsor Castle, diaries hidden in attics in Scotland, a job in New York, a fellowship in Boston, and a career in journalism.



Journalism and history are closely related; the former is the messy first draft of the latter. Neither of them is ever perfect. Both require constant revision, vigilance, revisitation. And both require attention. Most importantly, attention to detail. Accuracy is everything for journalists. And for historians, for whom the challenge is not just to notice and record what’s there but also what’s missing. Related Article Vale Former NSW and federal MP Bruce Baird given ‘one last upgrade’ in grand Sydney farewell The key is observation. Intense, slow observation. One of my favourite historians, David McCullough, has four words pinned above his computer in his writing shack in Martha’s Vineyard: “Look at the fish”. This comes from Louis Agassiz, the 19th-century Harvard naturalist, who would give every new student the same test. He’d pluck a smelly fish out of a jar and tell them to just look at it. Many stared at it for days. One of them wrote that after several days of despair he realised what he had not seen, and what was unique. Excitedly, he said to Agassiz, “It has paired organs, one on either side!” “Great, that’s right, you’ve got it!” said the teacher.



“OK,” said the student, “what now?” Agassiz said: “Look at the fish.” Some spent months doing this. Related Article Opinion

Archibald Prize An open letter to Gina Rinehart, from Queen Victoria (who loved her beer) Julia Baird Journalist, broadcaster, historian and author The reason I love this story is because it underlines the power of true attention. Keep looking and you will see things others haven’t. Keep looking to ensure your eyes don’t deceive you. Don’t be freaked out if you notice something that others haven’t. This is where the study of history requires courage. And it’s even more important in an era of AI – a vaulting technology that is better and faster than any of us here at synthesising and charting every single thing that’s ever been noticed and recorded by humans. But noticing things that haven’t been noticed? Seeing gaps and wondering about them? That takes deep and meticulous human observation. I felt all the apprehension you could possibly imagine when I decided to write a biography of Queen Victoria, even though she was one of the most examined women in history. I kept staring at the fish. And I found absences, assumptions, mistakes others had made. I found a tiny scrawl in the margins of a diary of Victoria’s doctor that described a flirtation game where she and her handsome Scottish ghillie, a man she clearly loved, played hide and seek, alternately lifting his kilt then her skirt. The headline in the Scottish newspapers once I’d published my book was “Queen Victoria and servant ‘exposed’ themselves to each other”!



I saw – in Victoria’s handwriting – the secret instructions she gave her doctor for her burial. Her wish that a photograph of Albert and a lock of her own hair be placed in her right hand. And in her left, a photograph of John Brown and a lock of his hair – as well as his mother’s wedding ring, which he had given her. She then instructed her doctor to cover that hand in gauze to conceal it from her family. As a researcher, finding details like this gives you full-body chills. Find the things that give you chills – and don’t let go of them. They do exist, outside the inertia of screens. And don’t underestimate the joy of full immersion in another world, another life or century.



When I was writing the biography of Queen Victoria I went to her holiday house on the Isle of Wight. It was on my second trip, as I was walking through the yellow living room, slightly dusty from having seen Bruce Springsteen at a music festival the night before, that a guard whispered to me: “Have another look at that painting. Give it a really good look.” So, I stared and stared and stared at it – a portrait of three women lying on the grass under a parasol – and then suddenly I saw it: the outline of a man’s back under the skirt of the woman in the middle, and two extra shoes poking out. The man was hidden and the woman had a particularly dreamy look on her face. And this was the first painting Victoria gave Albert, which tells us a lot. Attention is our greatest commodity now, one that tech platforms seek to suck from us daily. Fight for yours. Hold it tight. It’s a great weapon.



Your attention is worth something. It’s worth everything, actually. Human attention is the building block of just about everything that is valuable in our shifting lives. Without sustained and very particular human attention in a discipline that is not my own, for instance, I wouldn’t be here today. My surgeon – Associate Professor Dr Cherry Koh, a colorectal surgeon from the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital, has conducted three of four massive operations to remove cancer from my abdomen over the past 11 years. Think of the attention to detail she must possess. Former NSW and federal Liberal MP Bruce Baird died aged 84. James Alcock / AFR My last surgery was 19 hours long. In this case I guess I was the fish. I marvel at her work and her skills. So, on that visit to Sydney University last week, I had one piece of advice for the students to whom I spoke: pay attention. Know the value of that attention. Deploy it wisely. Notice each other, notice the world, notice the appetites, desires and blind spots of your own mind. Ask yourself constantly, who and what has my attention? Is it worth it? Is my attention going to places that reward the investment? Am I harvesting knowledge? Awe? Insight? Is it useful? Attention is the magical, quicksilver asset of our age.



But most of all – look at the fish, just as my dear Dad used to do. This is an edited version of a speech given by Julia Baird at the University of Sydney. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaMass shooting Children aged 5, 8 and 11 killed in Oregon school shooting, police say Alanna Durkin Richer Updated October 16, 2026 — 11:47am ,first published October 16, 2026 — 10:12am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Bend, Oregon: Three children aged 5, 8 and 11 and a teacher were killed in a shooting at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, police said. The shooter, a 16-year-old boy, was found dead inside the school when police arrived on Thursday (Oregon time), Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said. A community member had pursed him into the school and shot him, Krantz said. Another child and teacher were taken to the hospital, Krantz said. A sheriff’s deputy walks outside Silver Rail Elementary school, where a shooting took place on Thursday. AP Photo/Joe Kline The shooting happened at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, a city of about 100,000 residents in rural central Oregon, south-east of Portland.



The first 911 call came about 1pm on Thursday from a person in a vehicle outside the school, who reported being shot at by someone with a long gun, Krantz said. Further 911 calls came from inside the school, Bend police spokesperson Sheila Miller earlier said. Police arrived on the scene within minutes and found that the suspect had been shot dead. Silver Rail Elementary serves kindergarten through fifth grade, roughly ages five to 11, in Bend, situated in the Oregon high desert adjacent to the Deschutes National Forest. It has about 450 students and 40 staff members, Miller said.



“We are stunned and heartbroken by this senseless tragedy,” said Bend-La Pine Schools superintendent Steven Cook. “We extend our deepest sympathy to the families and to everyone affected by this violence. No words can adequately express the grief our community is experiencing. Our immediate priorities are caring for our students and staff and assisting law enforcement and emergency responders.” Police outside Silver Rail Elementary school, where a shooting took place on Thursday. AP Photo/Joe Kline US Representative Maxine Dexter, a physician who represents a portion of Portland east of the Willamette River, called the shooting a “devastating day for Oregon”. “Schools should be places of learning, friendship and joy. It is incumbent on me, and every lawmaker, to do everything we can to ensure our kids are safe,” she said in a statement.



“As we learn more about the tragic event at Silver Rail Elementary in Bend today, we must come together and support each other, neighbour to neighbour, Oregonian to Oregonian. No community should have to live through this day,” Governor Tina Kotek said separately on X. FBI chief Kash Patel said on X that federal agents were on the scene “assisting our local partners in the investigation” and that his agency would “make every resource they need available”. Buses lined up outside the school. AP Photo/Joe Kline More to come AP, Reuters, Bloomberg Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Even Stephen Curry’s King Arthur can’t save stale Spamalot, plus other new shows this week
World.content:
Sydney Event Centre, October 15. Until October 18

There’s a scene early in Spamalot, where a man wanders the streets of a plague-ridden town in medieval England pushing a cart piled with lifeless bodies, shouting “Bring out your dead!” Lancelot enters dragging a body, which struggles out of his clutches crying “I am not dead yet”. Cue music for a jaunty song and dance number.

Stephen Curry plays King Arthur in Spamalot Ben Fon

“I’m not dead yet” is one of those classic Monty Python lines, greeted by laughs and cheers by a hyped-up fandom on the first night. But is there still life in the old thing? I’m not convinced.

Spamalot, subtitled “A new musical lovingly ripped off from the motion picture Monty Python and the Holy Grail”, was created by Monty Python original Eric Idle in 2006. It had a successful Broadway run, scooping up a fistful of Tony Awards. This Australian production, produced and directed by Drew Anthony, is a competent rehash starring Stephen ‘The Castle’ Curry as King Arthur and an enthusiastic all-singing, all-dancing ensemble.

Marney McQueen as the Lady of the Lake.

The plot is an undergrad rewrite of the Arthurian legend. God commands King Arthur to find the Holy Grail. Arthur recruits a motley posse of knights and, after a glow-up at Camelot, they grab their coconut shells (clip-clop, clip-clop) and set out. The quest takes them to France, where they meet flatulent locals, knights who say “Ni!”, and a Black Knight who is harder to kill than a cockroach. But do they find the grail?

Curry is not an obvious choice as lead but makes a good fist of the preening role of Arthur, despite his tortuous English accent. His sidekick Patsy, played by Jamie Rolton, who also choreographs the show, frequently upstages the king with his well-timed quips and genial stage presence. Marney ‘Titanique’ McQueen sings her heart out as Lady of the Lake, leaning into the diva energy of Whatever Happened To My Part?, while Gareth Isaac as Sir Robin bubbles with showtime glee while singing You Won’t Survive On Broadway Without Jews. Awkward.

Stephen Curry as King Arthur with the cast in a scene from Spamalot. Ben Fon

Drew Anthony’s design concept is a deliberate collision of low-fi production values and technological wizardry. The costumes are straight from the dress-up box, and dad made the props, while the backdrop (by Travis Badge of Aquixel) transports us to rolling hills and luxuriant forests, and even provides a fully digital cast member, the Black Knight, yelling “’tis but a flesh wound” as it spurts bloody pixels.

It’s not the cast’s fault that this show fails to dazzle: the gags are desperately dated and the music is derivative. That is not a guarantee of failure in itself – lots of musical theatre shows thrive on in-jokes and self-parody – but the many compromises, including canned music and a terrible venue, do nothing to lift the raw material out of its nostalgic soup. Without the bite of up-to-date satire and the zing of in-the-moment comic improv, Spamalot has no teeth. This one’s strictly for the fans.

Spamalot also shows at Coliseum Theatre, Rooty Hill from October 22-25.

Police have locked down part of Dulwich Hill in Sydney’s inner west after reports a man armed with a shotgun is in the area. Heavily armed tactical police, along with a police helicopter and general duties officers, rushed to the area near Williams Parade and Constitution Road about 10.30am on Friday, after gunshots were reported to emergency services. Police have shut down the area as they comb Dulwich Hill for the gunman. James Brickwood Police responded to reports of gunfire in Dulwich Hill on Friday. 9News Nearby businesses and cafés have been put into lockdown, along with Dulwich Hill Public School, as officers hunt the man who is allegedly armed with a sawn-off shotgun.



Witnesses on the ground told Nine News there had been an altercation between the man and another group of people, which ended in a car being set alight by an apartment complex. Tactical police, along with the police helicopter, are combing the suburb for the man. Nine News A Dulwich Hill café has been shut down, while locals have been asked to remain indoors. Nine News A large exclusion area has been established, as police search for the gunman. Locals have been urged to remain inside, while those travelling through Dulwich Hill have been redirected from the area. No injuries have been reported, nor have any arrests been made. Light rail services between Dulwich Hill and Lilyfield have been stopped amid the ongoing operation.



The operation comes after bullets were sprayed at a house in Sydney’s south-west at 12.35am on Friday, occupied by two men, 21 and 23, and a 59-year-old woman. Police responded to the house in Willis Street, Lansvale, before stopping a grey sedan at nearby Hollywood Drive. Officers allegedly found a balaclava and firearm in the car shortly after the drive-by shooting, before arresting its occupants – two males, 17 and 18, and a 17-year-old girl. The trio were arrested and taken to Cabramatta Police Station, where they faced police questioning. No charges have been laid. The occupants of the targeted house were uninjured. More to come

World.title: Principal admits ‘failures’ after anti-abortion speaker addressed Scotch students
World.content:
Breaking NationalVictoriaPrivate schools Principal admits ‘failures’ after anti-abortion speaker addressed Scotch students Caroline Schelle October 16, 2026 — 12:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
