The principal of one of the state’s most exclusive private schools has apologised after a controversial anti-abortion speaker addressed year 11 boys in a presentation that shocked students and staff. Dr Emma Wood spoke to the students in September as part of the school’s Christian education curriculum. Scotch College’s principal has apologised after a controversial anti-abortion speaker addressed year 11 boys. Wayne Taylor Wood runs the anti-abortion “Pro-Love Logic” organisation and gives presentations to help students understand the relationship between “widespread abortion and the individualistic sexual culture the West has embraced”. Principal Scott Marsh sent a letter to parents of year 11 students on Friday after he commissioned an internal review.



“I am ultimately responsible for activities involving our students,” Marsh wrote in the letter seen by The Age. He said the review found there were procedural failings in how the presentation was arranged and managed. “The presentation should have been classified and managed as an incursion because it involved an external speaker addressing boys outside the normal class timetable,” Marsh wrote. The principal said it was a clear failure in processes. “We are sorry for the distress this caused some boys and families,” he said.



Related Article Exclusive

Education Scotch College students and staff left reeling by anti-abortion activist’s lecture However, he did not apologise for the content of the speech delivered by Wood. Her presentations for high school students include defining abortion as “an act of harm inflicted on an unborn human being that both intends and accomplishes that unborn human’s death”. The all-boys school was established in 1851, and is the oldest secondary school in Victoria. Based in Hawthorn, it educates nearly 2000 boys from prep to year 12. From next year, it will charge more than $47,000 for year 11 students. The principal said in his letter that the review did not make any findings against individual staff members, but focused on what occurred, the procedural failings and how to address them.



“A further session will be held for the same year 11 cohort this term,” Marsh said. “It will present a different perspective on the topic and provide boys with a further opportunity to consider, discuss and reflect on the issues raised within their Christian education classes.” A source not authorised to speak publicly said Wood’s lecture had made staff and students feel uncomfortable. “Everyone was taken aback … it wasn’t a discussion,” they said. In a previous letter from the principal to parents in September, he said the controversial speaker was recommended by other schools.



It did not go into detail about which schools recommended Wood. Wood teaches at Campion College in NSW, which was investigated after its dean of studies and a senior history lecturer made comments supporting the White Australia policy. Wood, who holds a PhD in philosophy from Victoria University of Wellington and “specialises in bioethics and political philosophy”, according to her website, did not respond to multiple requests for comment. World.title: Climb this spiral staircase for the long lunch of your dreams
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

There’s the mood, attentive but casual and oh-so-warm, as though any worries you have can be allayed by simply shrugging off a coat. There’s the structure: a set menu (two courses early in the week, four on weekends) with few decisions required. Add oysters? Room for cheese? Where’s your thirst leaning? And there’s the food, of course. It’s all sourced locally, from growers known by name.

Up a spiral staircase, on the top floor of an 1858 building that was once the Daylesford grocer, there’s now a cosy dining room lined with artwork, arranged salon-style, on mustard-coloured walls. Stepping up the tight whorl is like spinning yourself into a fantasy: all your dining dreams are about to come true.

You can engage with this as much as you like: there’s no brittle culinary ego hovering and demanding you fall into silence with every lovely bite. Your informed waiter knows about the saucisson (perhaps crafted from Brooklands pork, a free-range farm in nearby Blampied) or the polenta (from corn harvested by Tumpinyeri Growers over yonder, milled on-site by co-head chefs Oliver Edwards and Bree Smith). But you can just keep sipping the wine (maybe the grenache from Dilworth and Allain, who have a cellar door around the corner) and sink into a reverie.

The menu changes weekly. That polenta might be the smooshy base for octopus

braised in red wine, or pork cooked in sage and milk, the latter from Tess Sellar, who runs a dairy herd of just 10 cows. It’s rustic stuff, made for eating, not Instagram. Even so, the salad gleams in its dressing, every leaf just so, and the roasted flathead flakes easily, as though a card sharp is dealing a royal flush, and the sweet cream squeezes lusciously from a crisp-crackled choux puff.

Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up

Roasted flathead, salad and potato bake. Bonnie Savage

Merenda turns five this month. Owners Andy and Clare Ainsworth are Sydney

escapees with backgrounds in hospitality and wine (him) and illustration (her). In 2020, they decided central Victoria was something of an antipodean Provence and built a life there, followed by a wine bar in Daylesford’s divey old pizza shop.

The first iteration of Merenda was beautiful and fun, though a little clunky, because there was no way to separate boisterous drinkers from special-occasion diners. The current space, inhabited a year ago, means diners are ensconced up those spiral stairs, while drop-ins are downstairs at the bar, where the food

is as good, just a little simpler. Maybe there’s duck: the grilled breast appears in the bistro with lentils and braised greens, while the legs are confited for the bar. Everyone wins.

World.title: December rare earths production debut looms for Lindian in Malawi
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears December rare earths production debut looms for Lindian in Malawi Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward October 16, 2026 — 12:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. ASX 300-listed Lindian Resources has the pedal to the metal at its Kangankunde rare earths project in Malawi, with construction hitting key milestones as it heads towards first monazite concentrate production in December. Kangankunde’s sheer scale has captured global attention, with the project considered one of Africa’s most significant rare earths deposits. It hosts a massive 261-million-tonne resource grading an impressive 2.19 per cent total rare earth oxides (TREO). Within that inventory is a high-grade core of 26 million tonnes at a hefty 3.7 per cent TREO, earmarked as the initial feed for the stage-one plant. Installation works completed across the Kangankunde process plant’s separation circuits ahead of commissioning at Lindian Resources’ Kangankunde rare earths project in Malawi, with first production targeted for December. The company says its construction and operational readiness activities are progressing on multiple fronts. Structural steel installation in the plant’s wet high-intensity magnetic separation and magnetic gravity separation areas is now 90 per cent complete. The installation of shaking tables is 80 per cent done, while the crucial regrind mill has been installed and piping is being laid. On the power front, the 33-kilovolt overhead transmission line has now been commissioned through to the transformer yard. Both of its 1250 kilovolt-ampere plant transformers have passed factory acceptance testing in Malawi and are back on site, ready to be fired up in the first week of November. Lindian says this will allow time for motor testing and electrical commissioning ahead of introducing the first ore to the plant.



‘Every milestone brings us closer to becoming a rare earths producer.’ Lindian Resources executive director Zac Komur While construction pushes ahead, mining operations have continued to swell run-of-mine (ROM) stockpiles. The company says it now has 149,000 tonnes of ore on the ROM pad, up 19 per cent from the 125,000 tonnes held in September. Mining has also moved to the pit’s upper levels, with drilling underway from the top of the hill to open up additional mining faces. Lindian executive director Zac Komur said: “Kangankunde is in the final stretch of construction. Our target is clear: first monazite concentrate in December. The plant is taking shape, ore stockpiles are growing and our focus is on completing the remaining work and commissioning safely. Every milestone brings us closer to becoming a rare earths producer.” Lindian’s push to become Africa’s next rare earths producer is playing out against a backdrop of intense global competition for the critical minerals. Rare earths have become a focal point of supply chain security, with the International Energy Agency warning that industries from automotive and defence to electronics face significant exposure to Chinese supply constraints. This has sparked a flurry of dealmaking, with rare earths accounting for more than nine per cent of global mining and metals transaction value in the first half of this year. Major financing and acquisitions have been seen in Australia, Brazil and the United States as the West tries to build out alternative supply chains.



Notably, stage one of the Kangankunde project is fully funded through to production, backed by a long-term strategic partnership and offtake deal with major mineral sands producer Iluka Resources. The project’s progress also appears to have the support of the Malawian government, which has a stated policy of encouraging in-country value-addition for its minerals before export. Importantly for the company’s social licence to operate, locals make up 85 per cent of Lindian’s direct workforce of 3000 people, overwhelmingly Malawian nationals, currently employed across the broader construction of the project. Lindian’s on-site concentrate production dovetails neatly with its broader downstream ambitions, having also acquired the SARECO mixed rare earth carbonate processing facility in Kazakhstan to capture more value from its Malawian product. The company has also locked in a partnership with French processing expert Carester to develop an oxide separation facility in Kazakhstan, along with a binding offtake agreement for its future high-value heavy rare earth products. This, combined with its portfolio of bauxite assets in Guinea and Tanzania, positions the company as an increasingly diversified international player with operations spanning multiple commodities and jurisdictions.



With the plant taking shape and power about to flow, Lindian is almost set for the transition to full-time operations. The first plant supervisor and two control room operators are on the books and operator training has begun. Key consumables have been secured and outbound logistics contracts covering rail transport and freight forwarding are now being finalised for execution ahead of the first shipment. As the clock ticks down to its December production target, Lindian appears to be in the box seat and speeding towards delivering a new, large-scale source of rare earths into a market that is crying out for supply chain diversity. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.title: Ukraine’s latest battlefield drone is about to enter the kill zone – to fly out the wounded
World.content:
WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war Ukraine’s latest battlefield drone is about to enter the kill zone – to fly out the wounded Samya Kullab October 16, 2026 — 11:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A secret location in Ukraine: Six propellers whir to life, lifting a drone above a field. A weighted stretcher secured to its frame simulates a wounded soldier in body armour. Far from the front line, the demonstration offers a glimpse of a far more dangerous mission: flying into a battlefield where enemy drones and artillery can leave wounded troops stranded for weeks or months, then carrying them to safety without an evacuation crew. Loading Some of the more harrowing footage to emerge from this war has been drone tracking and striking fallen soldiers with nowhere to flee. AP was granted exclusive access to a field demonstration of the drone. This week, StarGate was handed over to a combat brigade for evaluation under front-line conditions.



The aerial medical evacuation drone was developed over the past year by Ukrainian defence technology company SkyFall. If it proves reliable in combat, it could transform battlefield evacuations, reaching soldiers in places that ground vehicles cannot access and potentially saving those so severely wounded that hours of waiting could cost them their lives. “The idea came directly from the front line, from the trenches,” said SkyFall’s spokesperson, who asked not to be named because of the security risks facing Ukrainian military technology personnel. He spoke wearing a balaclava and AP was not permitted to disclose the testing location. The Associated Press was granted exclusive access to the StarGate demonstration. AP In some sectors, the so-called kill zone – the area under constant threat from drones and artillery – stretches 10 to 15 kilometres or further. StarGate has a one-way range of 15 kilometres, potentially allowing it to reach critically wounded soldiers trapped deep inside the kill zone. A request from a military commander



The idea grew out of a military request, the spokesperson said. Last year, “Flint”, commander of the 475th Separate Assault Regiment known as Code 9.2, approached SkyFall’s founder about developing a safer way to evacuate wounded soldiers from hard-to-reach positions. For troops in Code 9.2, reaching a front-line position to retrieve the wounded can mean travelling on foot through areas where vehicles are vulnerable to drones. Unmanned ground vehicles have taken on a growing role in evacuating casualties and delivering supplies, but they struggle through mud, craters and shattered roads. Rivers, mines and drones can stop them altogether. A drone pilot operates the new StarGate at an undisclosed location in Ukraine. AP Ground robots typically take two to three hours to reach a position, depending on distance, road conditions and the threat from above, said “KVN”, a commander with Code 9.2. “Covering 10 kilometres in minutes would be a drastic change on the front line,” he said.



Evacuations continue regularly in his unit’s area, he said, but it is not always possible to retrieve a wounded soldier on the same day. For someone with severe injuries, the wait can be critical. Both Flint and KVN were identified only by their call signs in line with Ukrainian military protocol. The StarGate drone, equipped with a medical module, deploys a net designed to intercept aerial threats. AP SkyFall emerged after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, and has grown into a Ukrainian drone manufacturer. Its Vampire heavy-lift drone, known to Russian forces as “Baba Yaga”, is used by Ukrainian troops for battlefield missions. The company also makes Shrike, a first-person-view drone, and has developed the P1-SUN aerial interceptor. Named after the science-fiction franchise in which portals connect distant worlds, StarGate can carry a payload of up to 150 kilograms, according to the company – enough for a wounded soldier wearing body armour and carrying combat equipment. Its medical evacuation cabin is built around a stretcher.



The drone cruises at 65km/h and can reach speeds of up to 105km/h. SkyFall says it can be prepared for flight in about 10 minutes. Duelling drone tests At the test field, StarGate lifts off as first-person-view drones buzz towards it, simulating the aerial threats that dominate Ukraine’s front line. Electronic jamming is activated. As one attacking drone closes in, a net shoots out, ensnaring it and sending it off course. Military medics treat a wounded Ukrainian soldier in the field hospital in the Zaporizhzhia region, Ukraine, last month. Ukrainian 65 Mechanised Brigade/AP The encounter resembles a futuristic duel fought by machines. But carrying a wounded soldier raises the stakes.



One of SkyFall’s biggest challenges was ensuring the drone could navigate when electronic warfare disrupts communications or interferes with GPS signals. StarGate uses two communication channels – Starlink and the company’s proprietary L-Link system – alongside an artificial intelligence-based system to help it maintain control when satellite navigation is unavailable. The drone is operated manually, but has several AI functions that allow it to operate in GPS-denied environments or when signals are spoofed or frequencies are jammed, the spokesperson said. A Ukrainian serviceman launches a drone towards Russian positions at the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region last week. Ukrainian 65 Mechanised brigade/AP If communication is lost entirely, SkyFall says, the drone can plot a route back to a safe area. It is designed to operate in rain and snow, with thermal-imaging cameras for nighttime missions. SkyFall also says it has demonstrated the drone’s ability to continue flying after losing one of its arms. The company has not provided data showing how reliably it can withstand damage under combat conditions. The drone began front-line tests this week.



From prototype to combat ready drone Related Article Updated

Russia-Ukraine war ‘Betrayed’: Ukraine leader denounces Trump for siding with Russia amid row with Musk StarGate has undergone multiple design changes, including detachable arms for easier transport, a medical-grade stretcher and improved software and defences. The company estimates each system will cost at least $US50,000 ($72,000), depending on configuration, and aims to produce up to 1000 a month by the end of 2026. For KVN, however, it is too early to judge. His unit needs at least a month of experience with the drone before it can provide meaningful statistics on its success rate.



“It’s a completely new method of evacuation,” he said. “It’s difficult to talk in depth about the pros and cons right now. We need to work with it more.” SkyFall confirmed the unit was evaluating StarGate but declined to disclose the results. World.title: What my father Bruce taught me, and why I’ll always stare at fish
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsHistory Opinion What my father Bruce taught me, and why I’ll always stare at fish Julia Baird Journalist, broadcaster, historian and author October 16, 2026 — 11:54am

October 16, 2026 — 11:54am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Last week I returned to the University of Sydney to accept an honorary doctorate. It was wonderful to be back at a place that shaped my life and the lives of my family; where I’d spent the best part of a decade studying arts, and some law, and then diving into history to write a PhD that took a ridiculously long time and caused clumps of my hair to fall out. History, like careers, like human lives, never operates in a straight line. It gets knocked out of shape by events, like all of us, like the human heart. Julia Baird speaks to graduates at the University of Sydney earlier this month. Franky Tsang On that day my heart was particularly dented because that place was also where my father, alongside my mother, studied arts in the ’60s. He went on to live a big life of public service, humanity and adventure. He died suddenly, before I was due to speak at the university, and I thought about not going. But I was there because he would have wanted me there, along with my family – mainly because he loved attention and fancy hats and would have been horrified at the prospect of my forgoing either on his account. Dad always said Mum was the great scholar, not him. Which may be fair. But he was a great human. And he paid attention, especially to the things that aren’t written down, that aren’t on the syllabus. He paid attention to people, and to the ocean.



He taught me to push forward in the surf, to enter the ocean every day no matter your mood or workload, no matter the colour of the skies, the size of the waves (within reason), to dive in and just try, to give it a crack. When you find people who believe in you, don’t take them for granted. Keep them by your side. Julia Baird and her father, Bruce Baird, in the ocean. I’ve worked most of my life as a journalist but history is the first great love of my life. History has sneaked me into the best places, like a friend who knows the bouncer (hang on to those people, too, by the way). History has taken me to secret archives in Windsor Castle, diaries hidden in attics in Scotland, a job in New York, a fellowship in Boston, and a career in journalism.



Journalism and history are closely related; the former is the messy first draft of the latter. Neither of them is ever perfect. Both require constant revision, vigilance, revisitation. And both require attention. Most importantly, attention to detail. Accuracy is everything for journalists. And for historians, for whom the challenge is not just to notice and record what’s there but also what’s missing. Related Article Vale Former NSW and federal MP Bruce Baird given ‘one last upgrade’ in grand Sydney farewell The key is observation. Intense, slow observation. One of my favourite historians, David McCullough, has four words pinned above his computer in his writing shack in Martha’s Vineyard: “Look at the fish”. This comes from Louis Agassiz, the 19th-century Harvard naturalist, who would give every new student the same test. He’d pluck a smelly fish out of a jar and tell them to just look at it. Many stared at it for days. One of them wrote that after several days of despair he realised what he had not seen, and what was unique. Excitedly, he said to Agassiz, “It has paired organs, one on either side!” “Great, that’s right, you’ve got it!” said the teacher.



“OK,” said the student, “what now?” Agassiz said: “Look at the fish.” Some spent months doing this. Related Article Opinion

Archibald Prize An open letter to Gina Rinehart, from Queen Victoria (who loved her beer) Julia Baird Journalist, broadcaster, historian and author The reason I love this story is because it underlines the power of true attention. Keep looking and you will see things others haven’t. Keep looking to ensure your eyes don’t deceive you. Don’t be freaked out if you notice something that others haven’t. This is where the study of history requires courage. And it’s even more important in an era of AI – a vaulting technology that is better and faster than any of us here at synthesising and charting every single thing that’s ever been noticed and recorded by humans. But noticing things that haven’t been noticed? Seeing gaps and wondering about them? That takes deep and meticulous human observation. I felt all the apprehension you could possibly imagine when I decided to write a biography of Queen Victoria, even though she was one of the most examined women in history. I kept staring at the fish. And I found absences, assumptions, mistakes others had made. I found a tiny scrawl in the margins of a diary of Victoria’s doctor that described a flirtation game where she and her handsome Scottish ghillie, a man she clearly loved, played hide and seek, alternately lifting his kilt then her skirt. The headline in the Scottish newspapers once I’d published my book was “Queen Victoria and servant ‘exposed’ themselves to each other”!



I saw – in Victoria’s handwriting – the secret instructions she gave her doctor for her burial. Her wish that a photograph of Albert and a lock of her own hair be placed in her right hand. And in her left, a photograph of John Brown and a lock of his hair – as well as his mother’s wedding ring, which he had given her. She then instructed her doctor to cover that hand in gauze to conceal it from her family. As a researcher, finding details like this gives you full-body chills. Find the things that give you chills – and don’t let go of them. They do exist, outside the inertia of screens. And don’t underestimate the joy of full immersion in another world, another life or century.



When I was writing the biography of Queen Victoria I went to her holiday house on the Isle of Wight. It was on my second trip, as I was walking through the yellow living room, slightly dusty from having seen Bruce Springsteen at a music festival the night before, that a guard whispered to me: “Have another look at that painting. Give it a really good look.” So, I stared and stared and stared at it – a portrait of three women lying on the grass under a parasol – and then suddenly I saw it: the outline of a man’s back under the skirt of the woman in the middle, and two extra shoes poking out. The man was hidden and the woman had a particularly dreamy look on her face. And this was the first painting Victoria gave Albert, which tells us a lot. Attention is our greatest commodity now, one that tech platforms seek to suck from us daily. Fight for yours. Hold it tight. It’s a great weapon.



Your attention is worth something. It’s worth everything, actually. Human attention is the building block of just about everything that is valuable in our shifting lives. Without sustained and very particular human attention in a discipline that is not my own, for instance, I wouldn’t be here today. My surgeon – Associate Professor Dr Cherry Koh, a colorectal surgeon from the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital, has conducted three of four massive operations to remove cancer from my abdomen over the past 11 years. Think of the attention to detail she must possess. Former NSW and federal Liberal MP Bruce Baird died aged 84. James Alcock / AFR My last surgery was 19 hours long. In this case I guess I was the fish. I marvel at her work and her skills. So, on that visit to Sydney University last week, I had one piece of advice for the students to whom I spoke: pay attention. Know the value of that attention. Deploy it wisely. Notice each other, notice the world, notice the appetites, desires and blind spots of your own mind. Ask yourself constantly, who and what has my attention? Is it worth it? Is my attention going to places that reward the investment? Am I harvesting knowledge? Awe? Insight? Is it useful? Attention is the magical, quicksilver asset of our age.



But most of all – look at the fish, just as my dear Dad used to do. This is an edited version of a speech given by Julia Baird at the University of Sydney. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Children aged 5, 8 and 11 killed in Oregon school shooting, police say
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaMass shooting Children aged 5, 8 and 11 killed in Oregon school shooting, police say Alanna Durkin Richer Updated October 16, 2026 — 11:47am ,first published October 16, 2026 — 10:12am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Bend, Oregon: Three children aged 5, 8 and 11 and a teacher were killed in a shooting at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, police said. The shooter, a 16-year-old boy, was found dead inside the school when police arrived on Thursday (Oregon time), Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said. A community member had pursed him into the school and shot him, Krantz said. Another child and teacher were taken to the hospital, Krantz said. A sheriff’s deputy walks outside Silver Rail Elementary school, where a shooting took place on Thursday. AP Photo/Joe Kline The shooting happened at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, a city of about 100,000 residents in rural central Oregon, south-east of Portland.



The first 911 call came about 1pm on Thursday from a person in a vehicle outside the school, who reported being shot at by someone with a long gun, Krantz said. Further 911 calls came from inside the school, Bend police spokesperson Sheila Miller earlier said. Police arrived on the scene within minutes and found that the suspect had been shot dead. Silver Rail Elementary serves kindergarten through fifth grade, roughly ages five to 11, in Bend, situated in the Oregon high desert adjacent to the Deschutes National Forest. It has about 450 students and 40 staff members, Miller said.



“We are stunned and heartbroken by this senseless tragedy,” said Bend-La Pine Schools superintendent Steven Cook. “We extend our deepest sympathy to the families and to everyone affected by this violence. No words can adequately express the grief our community is experiencing. Our immediate priorities are caring for our students and staff and assisting law enforcement and emergency responders.” Police outside Silver Rail Elementary school, where a shooting took place on Thursday. AP Photo/Joe Kline US Representative Maxine Dexter, a physician who represents a portion of Portland east of the Willamette River, called the shooting a “devastating day for Oregon”. “Schools should be places of learning, friendship and joy. It is incumbent on me, and every lawmaker, to do everything we can to ensure our kids are safe,” she said in a statement.



“As we learn more about the tragic event at Silver Rail Elementary in Bend today, we must come together and support each other, neighbour to neighbour, Oregonian to Oregonian. No community should have to live through this day,” Governor Tina Kotek said separately on X. FBI chief Kash Patel said on X that federal agents were on the scene “assisting our local partners in the investigation” and that his agency would “make every resource they need available”. Buses lined up outside the school. AP Photo/Joe Kline More to come AP, Reuters, Bloomberg Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Woman's body found after car plunges into water in Tauranga
World.content:
A woman's body has been recovered by divers organised by her family after the car she was in entered the water off Chapel Street in Tauranga early on Friday morning.

Emergency services were called at about 12.40am to reports of a vehicle entering the water near the Bay Central Shopping Centre.

The driver was taken to hospital after making his way out of the water. Police said it was initially unclear if there was anyone else in the car but further enquiries determined a woman had not re-surfaced.

"Family members organised their own divers to recover their loved one, and her body was recovered shortly after 8am today," Senior Sergeant Roger Schreuder said.

The Police National Dive Squad was expected to arrive at the scene later on Friday.

"Police remain at the scene making enquiries. This includes a scene examination, and forensic examination and recovery of the vehicle from the water, which the Dive Squad will assist with.

World.title: Manufacturing sector continues to grow
World.content:
New Zealand's manufacturing sector continues to expand, with production, new orders and employment all strengthening in September.

The BNZ-BusinessNZ Performance of Manufacturing Index (PMI) rose 3.2 points to 56.5, comfortably above its long-term average of 52.5.

A reading above 50 indicates the sector is expanding, while a reading below 50 indicates contraction.

It was the sector's 15th consecutive month of expansion and, putting June's exceptional result to one side, the strongest reading since 2021.

BNZ senior economist Doug Steel said the result showed the pace of manufacturing growth had accelerated.

Looking under the hood, the survey showed improvement across all of the survey's sub-indices as well.

Production and new orders both rose to 57, while finished stocks reached 59 and deliveries 58.8.

Employment remained the weakest part of the survey, but increased from 50 in August to 51.8 in September.

"Some signs of confidence are there that firms expect this expansion to continue and are hiring as a result."

BusinessNZ director of advocacy Catherine Beard said the stronger employment reading was encouraging.

"Employment also picked up, now back in expansion at 51.8, which is an encouraging sign that firms are perhaps starting to feel more confident about adding staff."

She said the strength in new orders, production and finished stocks suggested there was real momentum building heading into the final quarter of the year.

However, sentiment among manufacturers remained mixed, with 53 percent of survey comments negative.

Respondents continued to raise concerns about fuel prices and related cost pressures, uncertainty ahead of the election and the possibility of further interest rate increases.

Steel said despite those concerns, the improvement in activity was significant.

"Despite these things, activity is picking up, which is suggesting underlying expansion is underway."

World.title: 'This is what it looks like': Mayor speaks on city's water under-investment
World.content:
Audio player for " Wellington Mayor responds to growing water bill concerns " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/regions/1953363%2Fthis-is-what-it-looks-like-mayor-speaks-on-city-s-water-under-investment

Wellington Mayor responds to growing water bill concerns Morning Report Download MP3 5m

Wellington's mayor says decades of under-investment in water infrastructure is hitting home for the capital.

RNZ has revealed over 30,000 residents and businesses across the region - about 18.5 percent of invoiced accounts - had not paid their first quarterly Tiaki Wai bill, with the second round due to arrive from late October.

The water agency's chief executive, Michael Brewster, said the payments were in line with what he would expect given this was the first time people had received separate bills.

He said no penalties would be applied for late payment for an initial period, and no ones water would be cut off if they had not paid.

Wellington Mayor Andrew Little told Morning Report he would expect a new big water agency may have some "teething problems" initially, and the organisation needed to be dedicated to fixing networks, upgrades and ensuring safe water infrastructure.

"What is happening now is chickens coming home to roost from decades ago. So no one should be surprised about it.

"This is a generation that is confronting a problem that has been decades in the making."

Little said this was the start of the "long process of recovering decades of under-investment, so this is what it looks like".

The mayor said both the current government and previous government were trying to tackle the issue. The Local Water Done Well policy did not include central government funding to alleviate the price burden, Little said, while the previous government's policy did.

He said the government had been trying to recover long-standing under-investment in water infrastructure.

Little was asked about the pay of executives at Tiaki Wai, which includes a $645,000 salary for chief executive Michael Brewster.

"Look, they are an organisation set up under the Local Water Done Well policy that provide organisations run on a professional sort of basis with the right skills.

"What the board, the independent board does in terms of hiring staff is a matter for them, it is what it is," Little said.

Some residents have been shocked and concerned by the price trajectory of bills - which could reach over $6000 per decade, this prompted protests against the agency in August.

Little said he believed the Commerce Commission would have to regulate the agency's prices eventually, despite comments from the chairperson that it would not do that yet.

"I think as Tiaki Wai works out its pricing strategy over time, I expect we will need the Commerce Commission to exercise its price regulation power, we'll see how that goes," Little said.

World.title: Higher prices for fuel suggests inflation pressures have strengthened
World.content:
Higher prices for fuel and a range of other goods and services in September suggest inflation pressures have strengthened.

Stats NZ figures showed petrol prices rose 6.4 percent on August and diesel prices were up nearly 8 percent, as global energy prices remained elevated amid renewed US-Iran tensions and pressure on fuel supplies.

Prices spokesperson Nicola Growden said fuel prices had been gyrating since the Middle East war broke out sending prices surging at the start in March and april, then easing back in the middle of the year, before resuming the climb in August.

"Although prices in September were above March levels, they were still below the peak recorded in April."

Petrol was more than 24 percent higher than a year ago and diesel was close to 56 percent more expensive over 12 months.

Fuel prices make up about 4 percent of the broad inflation measure, the consumer price index (CPI).

Food prices flat - mostly

Food prices were flat for the month, but the annual rate edged up to 2.4 percent higher from August's 20 month low of 1.9 percent.

Fruit and vegetables were down 2.7 percent for the month, 1.8 percent cheaper than a year ago.

An 86 percent rise in onion prices over the past year, the highest on record, might bring tears to many a household, as would more expensive chocolate, restaurant meals, and food kits.

However meat and dairy product prices eased, which offset grocery price rises.

Food prices make up about 19 percent of the broad inflation measure, the CPI.

Electricity and gas, airfares, commercial accommodation, and rents all rose in price.

Inflation impulse stronger

ASB senior economist Mark Smith said the numbers, which make up about half the consumer price index, were considerably stronger than expected.

He calculated that prices of the measured goods and services rose 1.4 percent for the month, and even stripping out fuel and energy prices showed underlying inflation of 1.1 percent for the three months ended September.

"There remains a tug-of-war between cost pressures and economic spare capacity in influencing the core inflation trajectory, but at present higher costs appear to be winning."

Headline inflation hit a two and a half year high of 4.1 percent in the year ended June, and new numbers for the September quarter are due on October 22.

Preliminary picks are that the annual rate will edge lower, but Smith said that was likely to be only a temporary dip with resurgent fuel prices, higher building costs and airfares sending the annual rate back above 4 percent.

"The uplift in NZ fuel prices is looking increasing persistent with much greater risk that this follows through into wider wage and price setting."

World.title: Soft September for retailers Stats NZ data shows
World.content:
The latest electronic card sales data from Stats NZ shows spending in retail industries fell 0.4 percent, or $33 million, in September compared with the previous month.

Hospitality was the biggest driver of the September decline, falling $33m, or 2.3 percent, from the previous month.

Spending on apparel fell $6.7m, or 2 percent, while spending on durables was down $6.6m.

However, fuel spending rose $6.4m, or 1.3 percent, reflecting higher global oil prices.

For the three months to September, seasonally adjusted spending across retail industries was up slightly.

Statistics New Zealand said retail spending in the September quarter rose 0.1 percent, or $14m.

World.title: Call for criminal groups to be declared terrorists, as PNG police seize more high-grade guns
World.content:
Some Papua New Guinea parliamentarians are calling for tougher laws against violent criminals who they say should be categorised as "terrorists".

It comes as PNG police released details of a counter-terrorism operation in Southern Highlands province, in which they seized a cache of high-powered weapons and military-grade explosives.

Various districts in PNG have been experiencing a surge in activity by criminal groups, according to MPs during discussion this week in parliament.

Oro governor Gary Juffa said that in his province, criminal organisations have been engaging in "brutal, violent crimes, killings, injury to innocent people and disruption of especially health and education services".

"These criminal organisations, we are submitting that they be declared 'terrorist organisations' because that is essentially what they are doing - these are crimes of terror whereby they are disrupting government services deliberately and preventing our children from accessing these services, our women, our elderly people, our innocent citizens."

Juffa sought an update from Attorney-General Pila Ninigi over a submission to his office earlier this year from the Police Minister which asks for criminal groups targeting public infrastructure and government services to be declared terrorists.

The Governor of PNG's Oro Province, Gary Juffa, calls for criminal groups who terrorise the public and target government services to be declared 'terrorists', 14 October 2026. PNG Parliament

Ninigi, who is also the justice minister, said the government was looking into it and assured Juffa that the issue is being taken seriously.

"There are constitutional questions that need to be answered and looked at. If it needs to amend certain provisions in the constitution, we shall do so, and come through the parliament [to] make necessary amendments," Ninigi said.

In 2014, PNG's parliament passed the Counter Terrorism Act, which defines terrorism, prescribes what constitutes a terrorist organisation, and gives police and defence forces expanded powers.

Police counter-terror raid

Police this week said a counter-terrorism operation in Southern Highlands province resulted in seizure of factory-made weapons, ammunition and military-grade explosives in a raid on a business in Poroma.

"In particular, the discovery of C-4 explosive blocks and detonation fuses is extremely alarming, as this material has no legitimate use in civil society and is extremely dangerous," the country's police commissioner David Manning said.

"The threat posed by these domestic terrorist groups is serious, and poolice will continue to break open their networks, remove weapons and take suspects into custody to prevent them from undertaking attacks on vulnerable communities."

News of the seizure, which occured in late September, comes as police also seized a major cache of high-powered firearms and weapons manufacturing equipment in Port Moresby last week.

PNG Police Commissioner David Manning ANDREW KUTAN

"Criminals holding these explosives, along with assault rifles, shotguns and hundreds of rounds of ammunition pose a high terrorist threat and this is why we have new laws in place to deal with them," Manning said.

World.title: 'It's unfair': Energy pricing not fit for purpose for marae
World.content:
The case of a Taranaki marae that had a 400 percent rise in its power bill has shown how ill-equipped energy companies are to cater to the specific needs of marae, according to a Māori energy expert.

Ōwae Marae in Waitara saw monthly bills rise from $400 to as much as $2000 after a solar installation on their new wharekai.

Te Piringa Pūngao managing director Ruka Te Moana (Te Whānau a Apanui, Te Aupōuri, Ngāpuhi) was one of the experts who helped figure out what went wrong.

"We all know that marae are non-profit organisations that rely on koha to survive so you can imagine that going from $400 of running costs for electricity to two grand when you've just upgraded, spent a lot of money not only in a new kitchen but on a solar energy system and battery to sort that out. You can imagine how stressful that would have been on whānau," he said.

He said the largest share of the bill came from Ōwae being charged based on their peak electricity demand at events such as tangihanga, effectively charging them the same as a commercial entity despite sitting dormant most days - unlike a typical business.

"Where the pricing structure falls apart is when the marae are getting charged for these peaks that they might only have once or twice a month. They're actually getting charged for the capacity of those peaks for 365 days a year. That fundamentally doesn't make sense. It's unfair."

The marae also had an expensive 300kVA transformer installed, however Te Moana estimated it would only need a 50kVA capacity.

"So, a lot of things fell through the cracks there in terms of the EDB (Electricity Distribution Business), the electrical engineers, the installers. There was no communication, everyone just went off with a bit of paper, but there was no actual explanation. Then all of a sudden, the price has gone up."

Te Moana said the pricing mechanism just was not fit for purpose when it came to the need energy needs of marae.

"So on one hand, you're getting these [marae], they're electrifying then you're penalising them because the current pricing infrastructure is not in place to support that... In most cases, it's not the size of the solar energy systems that are getting installed, it's the increased load as a result of upgrades in facilities, and more often than not, kitchen upgrades."

Ko Tama Wahine the wharekai at Ōwae Marae in Waitara. Supplied

Te Moana said what happened to Ōwae was not an isolated incident. For marae wanting to electrify he recommended getting a feasibility study done to understand the size of connection the marae would need as a result of switching to electric.

"[Solar] is the best way to electrify and minimise costs for sure, but there has to be someone across all of that to guide them through it, so that EDBs don't take advantage and put assets out in the field that are not needed or are overspecced."

Secondly, you needed someone who understood how much capacity was still needed to draw up from the grid and therefore what capacity transformer was needed, he said.

"Experiences like this make marae want to go fully off the grid, which is fine because they avoid these charges, but what it does is that it makes sure they're totally reliant on their batteries, it means that they can't use the grid for a backup, and then more importantly though it means that they can't share via the grid, they can't share any excess energy that they have with whānau."

Report outlines potential benefits of electrifying marae

Earlier this week Rewiring Aotearoa published their Te Whakahiko i ngā Marae report, outlining that marae face rising electricity and gas prices, irregular demand, ageing buildings, and an energy market that is complex to navigate.

Rewiring Aotearoa community activator Matt Newman told RNZ there were benefits to electrifying marae, it could reduce day-to-day running costs and significantly lower the emission footprint of a marae.

"But perhaps more importantly, as we're seeing across Aotearoa, is actually the resilience factor. You know, we know that marae open their doors in every situation whether it's a storm or a flood or whatever else. And we're seeing marae all across the country doing that. And the ability for marae to keep the lights on, keep the hot water on and to be able to cook as well are really important."

The key technical challenge to electrifying marae is that marae are so varying in their energy use, from remote rural marae that might be used a couple of times a month all the way up to urban marae operating services every day, he said.

The Rewiring report modeled six marae in two sizes and three levels of use, all running on LPG bottles, then switched their heating, hot water and cooking to electric.

"If we were to electrify the gas heating and the water heating and the cooking in marae, I think that could save somewhere between $6000 to $23,000 annually off the operating costs. And that's the key thing there is that, yes, there is always an expense to the upgrade, but often these upgrades are happening through either iwi entities or through funding agencies," Newman said.

However, as the case of Ōwae has highlighted, the electrification of marae could lead to unintended consequences, particularly if the right support was not given, he said.

"For marae, however, there aren't a huge amount of places where they could turn to unless they're engaging professional services around electrification. We know that that hasn't often been in the funding piece either. You know, funders will happily fund upgrades for marae, but they won't fund the due diligence that's necessary to support marae in making really good decisions for the long-term future."

Newman said there had been a failure in the duty of care to Ōwae.

World.title: Suspected copper thieves cause major internet outage in Bay of Islands
World.content:
A second major internet outage in a week caused by suspected copper thieves is another blow to Bay of Islands businesses trying to recover from a slow winter.

The outage has affected 750 homes and businesses in the wider Russell area, leaving shops, hotels and the town's crucial ferries unable to take electronic payments.

Chorus' outage website shows the incident occurred at 1.27am on Friday.

The company said technicians were preparing the damaged cables for splicing and would start work once access was available.

There was no estimate as yet for the restoration time.

Anton Haagh, co-owner of the Duke of Marlborough Hotel, said only about 5 percent of customers paid with cash - so losing the internet was a huge disruption.

He said copper thieves had also caused a major outage on Monday.

"So it's the second time this week. We're about to go into cruise ship season. We've got wedding season coming up. We had a 15 percent drop-off in domestic trade this winter. It's been a tough winter and this is the last thing everyone needs."

Haagh said staff had rushed home this morning to bring in their own Starlink units to get the hotel's Eftpos back up and running.

However, for businesses with no access to satellite internet, it could mean losing a day's income.

The Duke of Marlborough Hotel in Russell is one of the businesses affected by the internet disruption.

For the hotel it meant a lot of extra time and hassle.

It would also make it harder for people to get to Russell because the ferries relied on electronic payments.

"They'll struggle to get people to pay the fares. It just cascades through the economy, particularly the tourism economy."

If the thefts and outages continued the hotel would have to switch to Starlink, Haagh said.

"It's just another added cost that no one really needs."

Chorus' outage map shows the affected area covers the entire Russell peninsula, including Russell township and Ōkiato, as well as Rāwhiti, Waikare, Karetu, and State Highway 11 between Ōpua and Kawakawa.

A Chorus spokeswoman told RNZ the outage affected 550 fibre broadband and 200 copper services customers between Kawakawa and Russell.

Technicians were on site and working towards restoring services.

"Early signs point towards vandalism of our cables, and we've reported it to the police. Our priority right now is to restore connectivity as quickly as possible," she said.

The company apologised for the disruption and thanked customers for their patience while the damage was repaired.

The latest internet outage has prompted Northland MP Grant McCallum to call for action against copper thieves - and any dodgy scrap dealers buying stolen metal.

"This is beyond frustrating. People targeting copper are damaging fibre cables and cutting off essential services to entire communities," he said.

"It's not just an inconvenience. Businesses rely on internet connections to process Eftpos payments, take bookings and serve customers. Families need reliable connections to work, access services and stay in touch. When the network goes down, the impact is enormous."

McCallum said Chorus had told him that copper and fibre cables were often located together, meaning people targeting copper could also damage the fibre network, causing widespread disruption.

"With the cruise ship season upon us and tourism businesses gearing up for a busy summer, the last thing Russell and Bay of Islands operators need is repeated internet outages," he said.

"And let's be clear, this is not Chorus's fault. Their teams are left repairing damage caused by vandals, while residents and businesses are left dealing with the consequences."

He said attention also had to turn to where stolen copper was ending up.

"We need to look at who is purchasing stolen copper and make sure those knowingly dealing in stolen material are held accountable. Scrap metal dealers have an important role to play. If someone turns up with suspicious quantities of copper cable or piping, questions need to be asked about where it has come from," he said.

"Legitimate dealers should be working with police to report suspicious sellers. We need to make it harder for thieves to turn stolen copper into cash."

It's not just communications infrastructure that has been damaged by copper thefts in the Far North.

Last month the Far North District Council was forced to close public toilets at Tii Beach and Te Haumi, both in Paihia, after copper pipes were stolen.

The toilets have since been repaired usng pipes made from other materials.

And in July a century-old bronze bell was stolen from St Charles Borromeo Catholic Church in Rāwene.

World.title: Supercars to return to Phillip Island, plugging hole left by MotoGP exit
World.content:
Supercars will return to Phillip Island from next year, helping plug an economic gap left by the loss of the MotoGP to Adelaide.

Victorian Major Events Minister Anthony Carbines today announced a five-year deal to host a Supercars Championship final series round.

It will be the first time since 2019 that the island has hosted Supercars.

Phillip Island will host its final MotoGP from October 23 to 25.

The track has hosted the event since 1989, but lost it to South Australia after the Victorian government rejected a request to move it from Phillip Island to Melbourne's Albert Park.

It later lost the Australian round of the FIM Superbike World Championships, which will be held on Phillip Island for the last time in 2027.

The loss of the two events has created anxiety in the local business community, which relies heavily on tourism from the events.

Local tourism body Destination Phillip Island says racing is worth $80 million to the local economy.

Phillip Island will host a Festival of Motoring in March next year, with Labor and the Coalition both promising to back the event.

Opposition major events spokesperson David Southwick today said the Coalition would provide $100,000 to fund the event if it wins November's state election.

World.title: World Cup opener a reminder of Test rugby league's glory days
World.content:
The Sydney Football Stadium is as modern a football temple as you'll find, but Australia's opening match in the 2026 Rugby League World Cup was like a trip back in time.

The game against New Zealand was played in the shadow of the Sydney Cricket Ground, where the Kangaroos have played ever since rugby league arrived in Australia in 1908.

It remains the site of so many sepia-toned memories of furious, blood-and-thunder battles because Test matches were the biggest, best and most brutal spectacles the game had to offer.

They would give these matches names like the Rorke's Drift Test or the Swinton Massacre, making them sound like wars.

Aussies win, Ponga suffers suspected broken arm Australia has won an all-time Rugby League World Cup classic, with a hat-trick from debutant Jack Bostock earning a thrilling 24-22 win over New Zealand.

Those days are past, swallowed by the twin beasts of State of Origin and the ever-expanding club competition, but last night's 24-22 win for Australia is proof they can live again, even if only for a night.

The crowd of 41,225 was the biggest attendance for any Test match in Sydney since 1974, and this was a game that reminded everyone of how it used to be as the two teams put on an utter classic.

The journey to the green and gold's victory was studded with indelible moments like Casey McLean's acrobatic opening effort and the twin length-of-the-field intercept efforts from Jack Bostock and Tom Trbojevic.

Tom Trbojevic scored one of Australia's two length-of-the-field intercepts. (Getty Images: Matt King)

But none were better than Kalyn Ponga's three battles with Reece Walsh, which were the kind of one-on-one duels that exist in the brief moments when a team game becomes an individual sport.

If they were gunslingers, this would have been high noon.

Walsh won their first meeting, bundling Ponga over the sideline in a try-saving tackle after the Kiwi debutant made a break in the first half.

But Ponga's revenge was beautiful. In the second half, after slicing through again, he left Walsh chasing ghosts with a left-foot step they should write songs about en route to scoring his second try of the night.

It was a glorious moment, but few bathe in glory like Walsh.

His reply was a length-of-the-field effort in which he stepped Ponga and Jahrome Hughes so comprehensively they ran into each other.

It was a gut-busting effort from Walsh, literally. He went for the technicolour yawn afterwards, so much so that Latrell Mitchell had to take the sideline conversion.

In the end, it was Bostock's third try, the Dolphin flyer's debut for good measure, sealing the deal for Australia as the World Cup began with one of the best matches — NRL, Origin or otherwise — of recent times.

It was a spectacle a long time coming. This was the Kangaroos' first game at the new SFS, which has been open for four years.

It was their first game against New Zealand in Sydney since 2014, and they'd only played there twice in the past decade before last night.

That absence began as a symptom of the decline in fan interest in the national side — the punters just stopped showing up — until it became a cause.

Jack Bostock was magnificent in his Test debut. (Getty Images: Matt King )

Taking the show on the road is important, and in recent years Australia has played all across its own land and beyond. They are a team for the nation, not just for the cities with the big, fancy stadiums.

But to stay in people's hearts and minds, to feel large in the life of a sport, to remind them how big this can be and how important it's supposed to feel, sometimes you need to play the old songs, the ones everyone used to know, in the big house.

Australia has so many wins it's hard for them to stand out, but this one will. Apart from Bostock's two aerial efforts, every try they scored originated inside their own quarter as they ran to victory from the back of beyond.

New Zealand will be filthy with itself for losing a game where its vaunted forward pack did everything it was expected to do as it trampled all over Australia.

Australia and New Zealand are expected to meet again in the final. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

The Kiwis finished with five line breaks to one, and more than 300 extra run metres. They scored 22 points but left more on the board with some sub-par execution in the attacking 20.

A poor end to a set from Hughes, who had plenty of time on the last inside the red zone but came up with a kick that led to a seven-tackle set before Bostock's leap to heaven, will loom large in their minds.

Against Australia, even if they lose a key player like Mitchell Moses to injury, even if their forwards get bashed, and even if they're the better team for great swathes of the game, you cannot ever give them an inch.

They can and will get better. After talk about the Kiwis and the Pasifika nations dominated the lead-up, Australia reminded us all that it is still its tournament to lose.

Tom Bostock was man of the match in a famous Test debut. (Getty Images: Matt Kind )

A rematch between these two in the final seems likely, but it's a long road to get there. Ponga's late departure with a suspected broken arm might put paid to the Kiwis' chances of claiming a second World Cup.

But before we look to the future, let us sit in the present a little longer as we bask in this glorious reminder of the past.

This was the good stuff. This is what it's all about. This is how it used to be and perhaps can be again.

One great match does not make a World Cup, and the international game cannot be taken back to its most legendary nights in just 80 minutes, no matter how good they might be.

Rugby league needs more of this: the best teams in the world, filled with the best players dancing on the edge of the blade, in the biggest and best stadiums when the stakes are highest.

It's a simple recipe, but the appetite for it is mighty. The crowd alone is proof of that, and there should be more of it to come.

Samoa and Tonga are almost certain to provide it when they play the latest round of a rivalry older than time in their sold-out pool match in a fortnight.

Less can be more for Rugby League World Cup The Rugby League World Cup exists in a constant state of change but ahead of the tournament opener between Australia and New Zealand the much-maligned tournament can prove less can be more.

The semifinals, which will almost definitely pit Australia and New Zealand against one of the two island nations or England, have the potential to be like the tournament opener.

In rebuilding the prestige of international football — its oldest treasure — the sport can strike gold again.

Rugby league gave up that prize once when it took Test matches for granted for years.

What happened last night gives it an electrifying shot in the arm and a taste of what it gave up, a sin this epic Australian victory proves would be madness to repeat.

World.title: Wallaroos believe 'possibilities are endless' ahead of 2029 World Cup
World.content:
Like every Test rugby player, Wallaroos lock Kaitlan Leaney knows a team cannot be defined by anything less than an 80-minute performance.

But on the recent WXV Global Series tour of Great Britain and France, Leaney feels the Wallaroos gave glimpses of the team they can be ahead of the 2029 Women's Rugby World Cup, which Australia will host.

The Wallaroos' 48-15 loss to England in Salford last month is a case in point.

Why Wallaroos are 'family' Past and present Wallaroos players reflect on the journey and challenges to reaching 100 Tests.

The final scoreline suggests a thrashing, but it does not tell the story of the first half when the Wallaroos held the upper hand over the world champions.

England did not hit the front on the scoreboard until the 46th minute after the Wallaroos led 10-5 at half-time.

"That first half just showed the potential that we have as a squad," Leaney told ABC Sport.

"I don't think it came down to England being rusty, or us having a few more games under our belt before we played them.

"I think it came down to us having that pure intent. We knew the way we wanted to play.

"We were physical on both sides of the ball. We spoke about winning the collision, and I think that we definitely did that."

The Wallaroos' Allana Sikimeti (right) takes on England's defence last month. (Getty images: Lewis Storey)

It was not just the Wallaroos' brute force that gave them the advantage, but also their intelligent strategy.

Faliki Pohiva's 31st-minute try came after the Wallaroos identified weaknesses in England's defensive formation and line-out.

"England is the best in the world and we took it to them for 45 minutes," said Leaney, who has been among the Wallaroos' most consistent players in 2026.

"We're definitely not happy with just that. We want to be able to come away with wins, but I think it just shows the growth and the capabilities we have."

Kaitlan Leaney has been one of the Wallaroos' best players this year. (Getty Images: Ian MacNicol)

A 29-26 defeat to world number four France in Aix-en-Provence the following week also provided encouraging signs, although the match was there for the taking.

The seventh-ranked Wallaroos failed to land the decisive blow, having squandered a 19-0 lead against a French side reduced to 11 players at one stage during the first half.

They rebounded seven days later to defeat Scotland 30-10 in Edinburgh; however, Leaney and her teammates were dissatisfied with their display after trailing 10-5 at half-time.

"In the first half, I think we let ourselves down in terms of discipline and missing some key opportunities that we created," Leaney said.

'Possibilities are endless'

The establishment of a full-time Wallaroos program is in progress, and will be a game-changer for women's rugby in Australia.

England invested wisely when it first offered full-time contracts in 2019, and it is little surprise the Red Roses have not lost a match in four years.

The Wallaroos are chasing back-to-back wins over Scotland. (Getty Images: Ian MacNicol)

A veteran of 43 Tests, Leaney knows the Wallaroos will improve immensely once they are no longer semi-professional.

"I think once we have that and we're together full-time, you'll see the results come from that," she said.

"I think the possibilities are endless in that space."

Wallaroos lose star for Scotland Test The Wallaroos are forced to reshuffle their backline for Saturday's Test against Scotland at Sydney's Stadium Australia.

The Wallaroos' immediate focus is tomorrow's WXV Global Series Test against Scotland in Sydney.

It is the first of two Tests against the Scots on Australian soil, with the second match to be played in Canberra on October 23.

Winning is the obvious goal, but Leaney is also determined that the Wallaroos produce a complete performance across both halves.

"That's something we're working on for this weekend and making sure we're firing from the get-go and sticking to our game plan," she said.

"Because when we do, it works. We just need to do it from the start.

"We just haven't reached that 80-minute performance yet."

World.title: De Minaur falls to world number one Zverev in Shanghai
World.content:
Top-ranked Alexander Zverev said he felt good on court after beating Alex de Minaur 6-4, 6-4 at the Shanghai Masters.

Behind his impregnable serve, Zverev, who is guaranteed to end the year as the top-ranked men's player after a season-ending injury to Jannik Sinner, enjoyed his most clinical match of the tournament after struggling with foot problems in earlier contests.

Zverev made 80 per cent of his first serves and saved all five of the break points he faced as he set up a semifinal meeting with Alejandro Davidovich Fokina.

"I felt both of us were playing really, really well. I was a lot of times out-hitting Alex, which is difficult to do from the baseline because he is so fast and he loves this kind of court speed here," Zverev said.

"I felt good, and I'm happy with the step up from the last couple of matches."

World number nine de Minaur, one of the best returners in the game, managed to eke out five break points over two key games, one in each set, but was then thwarted by Zverev's delivery.

After being broken for 3-2 in the opening stanza when the German unleashed a series of monster forehands, de Minaur immediately hit back in the next game by carving out three break points, only for Zverev to pound down five unreturnable serves in a row.

Having wrapped up that set in 37 minutes, Zverev then found himself under pressure from the Sydneysider in the second stanza as de Minaur earned two break points, sniffing an opportunity to move into a 4-2 lead.

Again, though, Zverev rescued the situation with fine serving and immediately broke a deflated "Demon'' in the next game to effectively seal the deal, earning his ninth win over the Australian, this time with 10 aces and 14 searing winners.

It continued de Minaur's depressing record against the German, having beaten Zverev only four times in team competition but never in an individual tournament.

The consolation for de Minaur, though, is that he ends another promising tournament by improving his chances of reaching the end-of-season, eight-man ATP Finals for the third straight year as he has moved up to seventh in the live Race to Turin standings.

That leaves him sixth overall, with Sinner's season already over because of his knee injury.

AP/AAP

World.title: Builder revealed, but cost of new stadium still 'being worked through'
World.content:
The head of the government body tasked with delivering a new stadium in Hobart has acknowledged that "cost pressures" could impact the final price tag of the project.

The construction of a 23,000-seat, roofed stadium is a key requirement for the entry of the Tasmania Devils into the AFL and AFLW competitions in 2028.

The project is currently budgeted at $1.13 billion, but that estimate is now more than a year old.

Builder chosen for Hobart's stadium The company that built a 30,000-seat arena in Christchurch, New Zealand, has been selected to construct Hobart's new roofed stadium.

Since then, construction costs have increased significantly because of the war in the Middle East.

Macquarie Point Development Corporation chief executive Anne Beach said further work would now be done to finalise the cost before the contract is signed by the end of the year.

"Through this next stage an important part of that is moving from the target construction sum to actually locking down the lump sum that will go into the contract," Ms Beach said.

"The stage two process will end in around mid-November.

" We'll then go through an assessment, and that's when we'll be coming back to government to discuss that cost. "

Loading...

On Thursday, BESIX Watpac was announced as the preferred builder of the stadium.

Ms Beach said "cost pressures" would play a part in the outcome.

"We'll need to consider, as we go through this process, cost pressures that are in the market and the cost to build as at today.

"We'll be continuing to analyse that, and we'll provide an update once we can after stage two."

At a press conference, Jeremy Rockliff did not take up the chance to promise Tasmania's input to the stadium would be limited to $875 million. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Premier Jeremy Rockliff said the final cost would be publicly revealed shortly before the contract is signed.

But when asked whether he could promise the state's input would be limited to $875 million, as previously flagged, he repeatedly skirted the question.

"We're working through a very rigorous process," Mr Rockliff said.

"We're at stage one, and we're working through and continuing that to get to stage two and, of course, signing the contract.

" And I'm not going to detail costs — they are being, they continue to be, worked through. "

Work is being done at the Macquarie Point site in preparation for the stadium construction. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Cost will be 'quite north' of $1.13b, MLC says

The state government's $875 million funding cap was part of its agreement with independent MLC Bec Thomas, who voted in favour of the development in December last year.

As part of that agreement, any further funds required to build the stadium would either be clawed back via "value management", a reduction in scope, or be sought from either the federal government, AFL or Cricket Australia.

The Greens remain sceptical the stadium can be built within the current funding envelope.

"We don't trust the premier and his commitment to stick to $875 million," Greens MP Vica Bayley said.

"That's why it's incumbent upon him to be transparent about where the additional money is going to come from and how parliament is going to be involved."

Vica Bayley says the state government needs to be transparent about where extra funds could come from. (ABC News: Owain Stia James)

Independent MLC Meg Webb said it would be "naïve" to think the cost of building the stadium won't be more than envisaged last year.

"I think all of us can look at the world's events since then, can look at other costs that have clearly gone up and imagine that now we're looking at a full cost for this stadium that's somewhere quite north of $1.13 billion."

She urged the government to disclose the cost to parliament before the contract is signed.

"We know that Tasmanians would like there to be transparency around that cost and now that a builder has been announced, there's no reason for the state government not to come clean and be really open and transparent and give us the expected full cost of the stadium."

Meg Webb says it's clear the full cost of the stadium will be far more than the current $1.13 billion figure. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

Expert says Middle East conflict likely 'having impacts'

Kiri Parr is a construction industry advocate and senior fellow at the University of Melbourne Law School who lectures in the delivery of major projects.

She said it was common for large-scale construction projects to go over budget because of external factors and long timeframes that can significantly affect costs.

"An external war that drives up prices that's happened since you did your budget won't have been factored into that original budget," Ms Parr said.

"So, it's exactly the kind of external factor that major projects are exposed to and it likely is having impacts on the budget.

" The exact nature of how it all plays out over the next three or four years is unknown. "

BESIX Watpac built Christchurch's new 30,000-seat stadium at a cost of just over $530 million. (Supplied: One New Zealand)

Ms Parr said the key was to limit the scale of any potential cost overruns through good management.

"It's the importance of working very, very hard on your projects to resolve problems as early as possible and not allowing them to escalate," she said.

"The importance of experts, people who have experience on major projects."

The stadium is due for completion by the end of 2030.

World.title: How the joy of Pride is 'a form of resistance' against queer discrimination
World.content:
GWS player Tilly Lucas-Rodd says AFLW Pride Round is important to continue celebrating and championing while harmful attitudes towards queer people persist.

Lucas-Rodd, who is non-binary, said the joy and pride of the moment are an important counter to the discrimination queer people can still face in sport.

"I feel like we were getting to a place of more acceptance and now we're going backwards, and there's more discrimination, and more homophobia, and transphobia," Lucas-Rodd told ABC Sport.

First current AFLW player undergoes gender affirming top surgery Over the AFLW off-season, Hawthorn's Tilly Lucas-Rodd underwent top surgery, a gender-affirming procedure that involves the removal of breast tissue in essentially a double mastectomy.

They said this is particularly evident in online comment sections containing discriminatory rhetoric towards queer people, including, at times, AFLW posts on social media.

"People are coming out of the woodwork, and they're proud and happy to have these opinions, and they think it's okay, which is why I think it's so important that we still have Pride round, and show up and represent the community and challenge these dangerous beliefs with joy," they said.

"There's a time and place to be reflective on the harm and the negative parts in terms of, like, the discrimination we face and truly reflect on that and sit in that and be like 'this is not okay'.

"But there's also a time to use joy and pride and celebration as a form of resistance."

They have seen the impact representation can have on people's lives.

Last year, Lucas-Rodd went public with having had gender affirming chest surgery in an exclusive with the ABC Sport.

The top surgery was a procedure that involved the removal of breast tissue in essentially a double mastectomy.

Tilly Lucas-Rodd in the Pride guernsey that GWS will wear for the club's home game during Pride round. (Supplied: GWS Giants)

They received many messages from people after the story came out, with people sharing it had opened up conversations with family members and given them a better understanding of the gender diverse and trans experience.

"A parent at my school that I taught at was like, 'You being so visible shows that for young trans (and) gender-diverse kids you can be successful, because they're often so hard on themselves and they don't see a future that's bright,'" they said.

"They see hardship, they see discrimination, they see transphobia as their future, but then they see someone being successful, being championed, being celebrated publicly, and they can see a way forward for themselves.

This year, what makes Pride Round even more special for Lucas-Rodd is it coincides with their 100th game.

Over the past 11 seasons, Lucas-Rodd has played for four different clubs, including Carlton (2017-2020), St Kilda (2020-2022), Hawthorn (2022-2025) and now GWS.

Tilly Lucas-Rodd was an inaugural player for Carlton. (Getty: Adam Trafford/AFL Media)

"It is so funny," Lucas-Rodd laughed, noting in particular the years at Carlton when they had shaved sides and bun. "There's been so many eras.

"I've changed completely as a person, and it was guided by AFLW. All I've ever known (as an adult) is AFLW, and all I've ever really been overly passionate about in my 20s is AFLW," they said.

The environments of the league helped shape them, which, they say, is why Pride Round is so important: the welcoming rooms they've been in aren't the same for everyone in sport.

Tilly Lucas-Rodd moved from Hawthorn to GWS ahead of the 2026 season. (Getty: Kelly Defina)

They did a video with men's GWS player Tom Green earlier this week for the club's channel for Pride Round, during which he asked Lucas-Rodd if they ever struggle with using their platform.

It made them reflect on how they use their social media accounts — quite often championing trans and gender-diverse people playing sport and playing footy — and how it has created a two-way dialogue with more people in the community.

"When I speak to people or hear from people's actual lived experience in community sports, it's not safe," they said.

"And I was like, that's something I've only ever learned through more conversations around Pride Round."

AFLW Pride Round The Gold Coast Suns' Katie Lynch wants to see the power of the AFLW's dedicated Pride Round harnessed and extended across the whole code.

Lucas-Rodd sometimes thinks, "Oh, this is probably getting old; people are probably bored of it", when they speak about their LGBTQ+ experience.

"But then I have someone message me being like, 'Oh, my parents read this, they heard this, they watched your video, and that made the conversation easy for me.'

"And it takes you back to why it's so important that we still have Pride Round.
