Tech.title: White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia Was an Affiliate Marketer for a Fitness MLM
Tech.content:
Since her first appearance behind the podium this week, White House press secretary Katie Zacharia’s past has become murkier by the day.

A WIRED review of deleted social media and professional networking profiles has helped clear up at least one mystery. Zacharia’s online résumé shows a gap extending from 2013 to late 2023. For part of that time, she worked as an affiliate of Beachbody, a fitness company that ran a multilevel marketing operation she describes to WIRED as “sort of a pyramid scheme.”

Zacharia’s background prior to her emergence as a right-wing operative and pundit in recent years has been the subject of intense curiosity. Prior to joining the White House’s press team, she was a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, a communications adviser at President Donald Trump’s media company, and a commentator on Newsmax and Fox News.

Other parts of her professional background have come under scrutiny, particularly her legal work. According to her LinkedIn, Zacharia was an associate at the Zhong Lun law firm, known in China as a top-tier “red circle” firm, between 2011 and 2013. She also identifies herself on LinkedIn as having worked as general counsel for the nonprofit Fix California. Tax filings reviewed by WIRED, though, show that rather than working as general counsel for Fix California, Zacharia was in fact a fundraiser for the nonprofit.

On Tuesday, journalist Judd Legum reported that Zacharia—who, he noted, had been identified as an attorney in at least 18 appearances on Fox News—did not appear to have ever passed the bar. Since then, The Wall Street Journal has reported that she sat for the California bar exam but never passed—a finding WIRED independently confirmed. (On Wednesday, watchdog organization Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint with the State Bar of California seeking to investigate the veracity of Zacharia’s claims to be an attorney.)

WIRED was able to gain some clarity about other aspects of Zacharia’s professional history using a database of material leaked online and created by the open-source intelligence firm District 4 Labs. It contains details from a since-deleted LinkedIn account belonging to Zacharia, which listed Beachbody email addresses as two of her points of contact. A representative for the company told WIRED there was no record of her having worked there. In a phone call, Zacharia confirmed to WIRED that she had never been employed by the company.

Tech.title: Junji Ito’s Manga Horrors Hit Harder as Live-Action TV
Tech.content:
“It definitely makes you wonder truly who is the real monster in the situation.”

Director Yûta Shimotsu is describing events in a new episode of live-action J-horror anthology show Strange: Junji Ito's Tales for Sleepless Nights, but he could be referring to almost any episode.

The award-winning manga artist of the title, whose macabre short works are adapted into disturbing 30-minute bites, has a way of blurring lines between protagonist and antagonist amid his surreal nightmares.

Tales for Sleepless Nights aired its 12-episode first season on TV Tokyo this summer, and now HBO Max is bringing those eerie frights to US audiences. The first two installments “Lovesickness (Part 1 of 3)” and “The Bully” (previously animated for Netflix’s Junji Ito Maniac) are currently available, but New York Comic Con fans were treated to the US premiere of the episode “Face Thief” based on Ito’s story “The Face Burglar.”

“Face Thief,” which was previously turned into a Japanese TV movie in 2000, follows the new girl in school, Machida (Nanami Yamazaki), who encounters a weirdly clingy classmate named Kamei (Anna Hoshino). After she sees an identical-looking girl in class who claims she is not related to Kamei, Machida learns this changeling’s MO: “She befriends cute girls then steals their faces.” Indeed, Kamei’s face begins shifting during close conversations with Machida. This repulses the new girl at first, but when Kamei scares away some bullies by growing a third eyeball on her cheek, the two start to bond.

We will not spoil the outcome, but the filmmaker turns it into a biting critique of the conformity and peer pressure common in Japanese society. As he told the crowd after the premiere, “We have social pressure that we are supposed to not to be too different from others. Individuality is not very respected.”

Despite Shimotsu’s desire to shape-shift the story by “changing the ending so my live-action version was different,” “Face Thief” still manages to capture the slow burn feel of the original comic published in the pages of Monthly Halloween in 1987, the same year Ito’s famous debut Tomie appeared. That shōjo (for girls) manga magazine’s offshoot Nemuki (“Strange Stories of Sleepless Nights") inspired the new TV omnibus’s title.

Junji Ito himself, now a bespectacled 63-year-old, appeared before NYCC in a video message where he described “Face Burglar” as an early tale he came up with after several unsuccessful stories submitted to his publishers: “Not a ghost, just a unique condition inspired by chameleon camouflage.” Ito added that the new adaptation for Tales for Sleepless Nights was “brought to life by a fresh team of upcoming actors and directors. Rather than jump scares, it builds a slow creeping dream perfect for horror.”

Another means through which Shimotsu (Best Wishes to All, Shudder’s New Group) finds the essence of Ito in all the episodes he helmed is through stillness in the performances and camerawork that evokes the comic book pages. He told a fan that he hopes to push fidelity to the material one step further in season 2 by shooting at least one episode in black-and-white, Ito’s preferred mode of illustration.

When asked by a con attendee which of Ito’s works he would most like to adapt next, the director earned applause by answering Uzumaki, the groundbreaking horror manga which has been brought to the screen several times, including a recent 4-part anime series for Adult Swim. The latter version had a famously rocky production, with quality diving after the first episode to the point that the fourth installment had no director credit. A new live-action version would be incredible—and incredibly strange—in Yûta Shimotsu’s hands.

“I would love to keep creating very bizarre, unique aesthetics like Mr. Ito's work. That's my goal,” said Shimotsu. “I'm developing a Hollywood project, so see you soon.”

Tech.title: Kids’ Content Is Deeply Broken. A New Platform Wants to Fix It
Tech.content:
If you have young kids or if you know somebody who does, then you know about YouTube’s AI slop problem.

Videos targeted at children on the platform are often filled with bizarre and hyperstimulating content that’s AI generated. Not all of it is age-appropriate. These videos autoplay on endless, algorithmically curated streams punctuated by ads.

Maka, a new streaming app for kids aged 0 to 6, is positioning itself as an antidote to that concern. The platform has zero ads and doesn’t allow autoplay or endless scrolling, and its algorithms intentionally do not maximize watch time.

The company’s cofounder and chief product officer, Tanyella Leta, tells WIRED the platform is purposely abandoning the mechanisms that “turn children’s media into an engagement machine.”

Maka’s CEO and cofounder Isabel Sheinman adds that a lot of the streamers were built to serve adults, not children. “Kids were really the afterthought,” she says. Sheinman wants to set a much higher bar for what quality looks like in children’s media, which she says has been warped by harmful incentives. “Maka was built with child development science and children's behavior first and foremost.”

Launching today, Maka’s programming slate is a mix of licensed content from global studios and independent creators. It features 25 shows in its curated catalog, including Franklin, The Wiggles, Pocoyo, Vida the Vet, and Sesame Street. The platform runs on a subscription service, with a $15 monthly plan and a $107 annual plan.

It was during the Covid pandemic that Sheinman and Leta became obsessed with thinking about how to redesign kids' media. The solution? Every episode streamed on Maka is evaluated by child development experts through Imprint, a framework created with researchers at the Yale Child Study Center. The evaluation process, which examines everything from scene cuts to how fast-paced content is, maps child development across seven core domains. It looks for things like emotional regulation, kindness, how child-caregiver relationships are modeled in a story, and how a story might support critical thinking or language development.

AI-generated content has only added a new wrinkle to kids’ entertainment: videos are incoherent, have no plot, or contain outright misinformation but are packaged to look like learning. Some of it, as WIRED has previously reported, is disturbingly sexualized, featuring gore and other fetishes.

Michael Robb, head of research at the media literacy nonprofit Common Sense Media, says that on a platform like YouTube, slop videos that have the veneer of education sit side by side with carefully designed educational shows. Robb believes YouTube and other kids’ streaming platforms have not done enough to distinguish educational content from slop, which has only made filtering content harder for parents. “Platforms have taken steps to reduce kids’ exposure to age-inappropriate content, and that matters. But ‘not inappropriate’ is a very low bar. There’s a big gulf between that and media created intentionally with kids in mind.”

Tech.title: Democrats Are Gearing Up to Investigate the Trump Administration. It Won’t Be Easy
Tech.content:
As polls indicate Democrats could take back the US House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate, lawmakers are gearing up to investigate the Trump administration. But that may prove to be a difficult task, even with a majority in both chambers of Congress.

In late September, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) released a report on Elon Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency titled “DOGE: Congress and the Public Lack Assurance That Systems and Data Were Protected at Multiple Agencies.” In it, the GAO revealed that multiple executive branch agencies had refused to fully cooperate with investigators about the extent and nature of DOGE’s access to sensitive systems and information. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), which DOGE and the Trump administration gutted in the early months of the president’s second term, sent the GAO a letter accusing investigators of bias and alleging the report was “misleading.”

The report, just the latest example of the Trump administration seeking to dodge congressional oversight, raises questions about what—if any—avenues the legislature has to enforce accountability, or even access basic information about what the government has been doing.

“In a world where there is no shame, it’s hard to think of what Congress can do that doesn’t involve some coercion of some kind,” says Emily Berman, a law professor at the University of Houston. “Like withholding money or going to court.”

The GAO serves as Congress’ primary investigative body; its work is most often initiated by requests from Congress but it is independent and nonpartisan. It does not, however, have the ability to enforce laws or take on prosecution. Federal agencies don’t necessarily have to enact the agency’s suggestions but they are legally required to cooperate with GAO’s requests for information and auditing.

The GAO and a Democratic congressional aide who spoke to WIRED on the condition of anonymity, though, say that the agencies investigated by the GAO for the DOGE report—the CFPB, the Department of Veterans’ Affairs (VA), the Department of Education, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), and the Small Business Administration (SBA)—all, in one way or another, refused to cooperate with the investigation.

“We have experienced increased challenges in obtaining information from agencies over the past year and a half,” GAO spokesperson Sarah Kaczmarek says. “As this report demonstrates, when agencies do not provide requested information, it can limit GAO’s ability to provide Congress and the public with assurance that federal programs, systems, and information are appropriately managed and protected.”

Tech.title: ‘Nightmare Scenario’: Zero-Click Spyware Is Infecting Phones via Targeted Ads
Tech.content:
On Thursday, researchers from The Citizen Lab at the University of Toronto revealed a worst-case scenario found in the wild: spyware silently infecting targets as they browse past ads in their daily digital lives.

Dubbing the attacks “AdFection,” the researchers documented a campaign in which an Israeli-registered advertising firm allegedly connected to the servers linked to a spyware company and infected dozens of devices with its invasive malware. Citizen Lab believes this to be the first detailed technical evidence made publicly available of sophisticated spyware infecting devices via digital ads.

Zero-click hacks are a holy grail for attackers and catastrophic for victims, because they can automatically install malware on devices without requiring any interaction or missteps from the target. When sophisticated hackers have deployed rare zero-click attacks in recent years, they have often exploited vulnerabilities in mobile messaging and communication apps to infect victims. But attackers have also exploited the sprawling infrastructure of the online ad ecosystem to distribute malware, sometimes with little or no interaction needed from victims. Evidence of the zero-click spyware campaign that Citizen Lab’s researchers uncovered shows the two threats merging, underscoring the extent and urgency of the risk.

“AdFection allows operators to automatically hack specific individuals with mercenary spyware as they use apps or browse the internet,” says Bill Marczak, a senior researcher at Citizen Lab. “Someone who gets hacked like this would not see anything amiss. In fact, they might not even see any ad at all.”

The situation is so concerning, he notes, because there isn’t much that people can do to protect themselves from zero-click ad attacks other than blocking ads as thoroughly as possible on all websites and platforms—a fact that intelligence agencies like the NSA and CIA seem to know all too well.

Tech.title: Did AI Just Erase an Entire Swedish TV Show?
Tech.content:
Fans of TV4’s international edition of The Challenge, which features Swedish celebrities competing in physical and mental contests, will have to wait for another season. An AI agent reportedly deleted edited episodes of the show, and a TV4 backup system failure wiped out hundreds of hours of work.

The Swedish series was due to return on Nov. 22, but has been delayed indefinitely, TV4 said in a statement.

“We have to recut it from scratch. All the raw material is still there, and all that,” program director Mia Lindqvist said on the network’s website.

More from CNET

According to translated articles, the network denies an Aftonbladet report that an AI agent deleted the episodes. However, while TV4’s Lindqvist told the newspaper that an AI agent didn’t act independently, she did not deny that AI was involved in the mishap. Still, she blamed the failed backup system.

“The big problem is that (production company) Mastiff’s backup didn’t work,” she said.

A representative for TV4 didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

The program features stars of other Swedish reality programs, such as the country’s version of The Bachelor and Farmen, a reality show about (wait for it…) contestants on a farm. The Challenge: Sweden first aired in 2023.

AI is increasingly a part of editing and production workflows across movies and television, with entertainment giants, including Netflix, leaning on the technology to produce content more quickly and at lower cost.

If an AI agent were somehow responsible, that would seem to have negated any of AI’s time-saving benefits for The Challenge: Sweden and its production team, who now have to spend time rebuilding the episode edits that were lost.

Tech.title: World Timekeepers Decide to Kill the Leap Second
Tech.content:
Human timekeeping rests on two main clocks, and they don’t always run at the same speed. For decades, the solution was the leap second, a minor adjustment added to international time to keep atomic accuracy aligned with the Earth’s natural motion. But on Thursday, the General Conference on Weights and Measures, or the CGPM (abbreviated from its French name), voted to abolish the leap second, closing a long-standing chapter in global time sync.

Most modern clocks rely on Coordinated Universal Time, a hybrid system caught between atomic time, which flows at a near-perfectly constant rate, and astronomical time, which fluctuates as the Earth’s rotation speeds up and slows down. To bridge the gap, UTC periodically inserted a leap second to keep pace with the planet. But reconciling physical planetary shifts with precise digital systems ultimately created more technical disruptions than it solved.

Breaking time

Computers are sensitive when it comes to timekeeping. The last few times we added a leap second to UTC — in 2012, 2015 and 2016 – some computer systems couldn’t handle it. Of the three instances, 2012 was the worst, as adding a leap second caused issues that crashed websites and software platforms, such as Reddit, LinkedIn and Mozilla.

More from CNET

The speed of Earth’s rotation experiences small changes all the time. While we can’t predict exactly how fast Earth will rotate in the future, the conference wrote that there’s a 30% chance we’ll have to add a negative leap second by 2035 to keep UTC aligned with rotational time.

If adding a regular leap second was trouble, imagine what adding a negative leap second could do. The conference doesn’t want to risk finding out. So, potential future computer anomalies caused by UTC changes are a major reason why the leap second is going away.

“Industrial users and the synchronization needs of national critical infrastructures, for example, transportation, energy distribution, telecommunication, and space projects, require UTC to be continuous without any future adjustment,” the group’s resolution reads.

Moving forward

The official death of the leap second will be May 20, 2027, when continuous UTC becomes effective. A continuous UTC means that no more leap seconds, negative or otherwise, will be added to UTC going forward. This also means that UTC and rotational time will begin to drift apart.

The CGPM noted that allowing time measurements to differ by up to an hour will keep UTC stable for several centuries.

This means in the future, when it’s noon, the sun might not be at its highest in the sky. But, considering we’ve only added 27 leap seconds since the concept was introduced in 1972, any changes that occur within our lifetimes will probably be very small.

Tech.title: New Amazon Bee Personal AI Devices Will Listen and Record You
Tech.content:
Trying to remember things yourself is so yesterday — or so AI-wearable makers want you to believe. Amazon on Thursday announced two new products, the Bee Frontier and Bee Eclipse, which use AI to record conversations and then process them into “summaries, to-dos, reminders and insights.”

The Frontier can be worn on your wrist or your clothes, and the Eclipse attaches magnetically to the back of your phone. They are both from Amazon Bee, which is the company’s lineup of AI-powered personal assistant devices and software. Amazon acquired AI-wearable company Bee in July 2025.

There are several ways you might use the devices. Maybe you’re talking with a friend at the coffee shop about details you’ll want to remember later. The Bee Frontier — on your wrist or clipped to your clothes — can record the conversation and give you a transcript or summary, much like AI tools like Gemini can do during a business meeting. The Bee Eclipse, attached to the back of your phone, can record your phone calls and give you transcripts and summaries of your calls.

More from CNET

Just make sure you ask your conversation partners if they mind being recorded.

Amazon says you can also review memories to remember conversation details, and Bee can recommend personalized goals and actions, depending on themes or trends it picks up on.

“The more you use Bee, the smarter it becomes, learning your unique patterns, preferences and relationships, building a progressively smarter understanding of your world without demanding attention,” an Amazon spokesperson told CNET via email.

You can view all the output in the Bee mobile or desktop app.

The Bee Frontier costs $75, and the Bee Eclipse will cost $100, though the Eclipse is not yet available. Users can pick between two tiers of service: The free one allows you to get conversation summaries and recaps for up to 14 days, while the Bee Pro subscription costs $12 per month, which gets you a personal chat assistant and provides unlimited memory, integrations with Amazon, Alexa Plus and third-party apps and suggests to-do lists.

The Amazon Bee Frontier and Eclipse come in various colors. Amazon

Amazon Bee Frontier goes on wrists or clothes

The Frontier can be worn on the wrist or attached to your clothes. It’s made out of ultrasoft silicone and comes in three colors — lavender, sage and onyx. A fully charged battery can last up to seven days and uses USB-C charging. The device has dual microphones and advanced noise filtering for crowded and loud places.

Audio recording begins by pressing a button, and a light goes on to show that it’s recording. You can also configure it to stop if there has not been sound for a certain period.

Amazon Bee Eclipse attaches to phones

The size of a credit card, the Eclipse can magnetically attach to the back of a phone and comes in four colors — silver, midnight, honey and blush. A fully charged battery can last three weeks and maybe more, according to Amazon.

You begin and stop recording with the Eclipse by pressing a button, and an LED light goes on to indicate that recording is in progress.

Connecting with Alexa Plus and apps

Amazon said the Bee Frontier and Eclipse can connect to Alexa Plus, Amazon’s new AI-powered assistant, and also Amazon.com. So, instead of getting conversation summaries, insights and to-dos by looking at the Bee app on your phone, you could just ask Alexa Plus to read them to you.

When connected to Amazon, the Bee device can present shopping recommendations on the Amazon home page or in the Bee mobile and desktop apps. For example, say your friend recommends a certain book while talking to you. The Frontier or Eclipse will hear that, locate it on Amazon and show that listing to you.

You can also link the Frontier and Eclipse to other apps, such as Gmail, Microsoft Outlook and Google Calendar. Amazon said Bee devices can draft emails and create calendar invites based on recorded conversations. Bee devices can also connect to your Apple HealthKit “to build a more complete picture of your wellness,” Amazon said.

What about data privacy?

Amazon said it does not store recorded audio, and you can neither access nor share it. You’ll be prompted to get permission from callers when those calls are being recorded, but it is not mandatory — the recording will still happen.

Expect the AI accessories market to grow. “Who doesn’t want to stop forgetting names and dinner plans?” asks Jon Rettinger, a tech tester with more than 1.66 million subscribers to his YouTube channel. But Rettinger said that invasion of privacy could be an issue, especially for people being recorded by someone using the Bee Frontier and Eclipse.

There are 12 states in the US where it is legally required that callers be notified that they are being recorded, known as “all-party consent.”

“The people around you never agreed to any of it, and a little light on your wrist isn’t much of a warning,” Rettinger told CNET. “In California, you legally need everyone’s consent to record a private conversation, and I’d guess most people buying these have no clue. For a work meeting where everybody knows it’s on, great. Wearing it all day is a different story.”

Amazon says Bee Private Compute — a security system built into both devices — processes conversations inside a secure and isolated environment “where no one, including Amazon, can access your data.”

After audio is recorded and processed into insights in real time, it is deleted, Amazon said. No one can get to your insights data unless you share it, and conversation transcripts are encrypted and are not accessible unless you choose to share them.

You can delete transcripts and summaries whenever you want in the app.

Tech.title: Supreme Court Weighs Major Video Privacy Case
Tech.content:
It’s usually legal for an American company to gather your personal data and use it to target you with an , and many online companies rely on this to make money. But a data privacy case now before the US Supreme Court may upend the longstanding practice of personal data collection for use in targeted ads.

The case, Salazar v. Paramount Global, stems from a 2022 class action lawsuit filed by Michael Salazar. At issue is a free digital newsletter Salazar signed up for, which was published by 247Sports.com, a college sports news website owned by Paramount Global.

The website included a tracker that shared Salazar’s video viewing history with Facebook without his consent. Salazar says that Paramount did this illegally. But the federal law that Salazar says Paramount violated is a 1988 Reagan-era act governing videotape rentals.

More from CNET

Home video leak

In 1987, President Ronald Reagan nominated Robert Bork for a seat on the Supreme Court, though the nomination was famously rejected by the Senate. During Bork’s confirmation hearings, a writer for the alt-weekly Washington City Paper convinced the manager at a video rental store to slip him Bork’s video-rental history, which the paper published along with commentary on Bork’s film choices.

While Bork’s rental history was fairly boring, the story and its fallout eventually led Congress to pass the Video Privacy Protection Act. The law was created for analog media, but Salazar’s team argues that it also applies to digital media, such as website content. Essentially, if it’s illegal for a video rental store to share your customer information, why are tech companies allowed to do it?

“The Supreme Court’s decision in Salazar v. Paramount Global will affect the privacy rights of millions of people across the country,” Salazar’s lawyer, Joshua I. Hammack, told CNET via email. “Ordinary consumers might be shocked to learn how much of their online activity is tracked, disclosed, and sold. As I argued to the Supreme Court, the Video Protection Privacy Act was designed to give Americans control over our private information, even as companies like Paramount seek new ways to monetize it.”

Defining a consumer

Paramount’s argument centers on how a “consumer” is defined in the Video Privacy Protection Act, with the company asserting that the definition doesn’t include people who subscribed to a free digital newsletter. This was the reason the 6th Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the lawsuit.

“The Sixth Circuit correctly rejected that effort,” a case document filed by Paramount reads. “The court of appeals dismissed Salazar’s complaint against 247Sports on the grounds that Salazar is not a ‘consumer’ because he did not ‘rent, purchase, or subscribe’ to the delivery of any ‘video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials.’”

The National Retail Federation, Retail Litigation Center, Motion Picture Association, Entertainment Software Association, Meta and the US Chamber of Commerce have all written the court in support of Paramount’s position.

A representative for Paramount Global didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Why do I care who has my data?

Neil Richards, Koch Distinguished Professor and director of the Cordell Institute at the University of Washington School of Law, believes the Video Protection Privacy Act applies to this case and should be enforced.

“Regulating surveillance-based ads, whether by banning them, by giving people meaningful choice to opt out entirely, or through interpretations of existing laws like the VPPA, would be the single best thing we could do for the privacy protections of the average internet user,” Richards told CNET via email.

Although the act was enacted back when Blockbuster Video stores blanketed the country, Richards said the law was intended for future use.

“Congress intentionally drafted the law in a far-sighted way to protect the activity of private video-watching, regardless of the technologies or formats used to watch,” Richards said. “A win for Salazar would be a much-needed win for internet privacy and a much-needed pushback to the greed of surveillance tech companies.”

What could change with data tracking

Even if Salazar wins, any restrictions on tracking could be limited, as the case is specifically about whether it’s illegal to share someone’s digital video-watching history.

“I think that video content probably isn’t actually influencing that many ads.” Justin Brookman, the director of technology policy for Consumer Reports, told CNET over the phone. “Most targeted ads are like retargeted ads based on, ‘you looked at this product, and therefore the product’s going to follow you around.’”

Applying the act here probably won’t sink online targeted ads, Brookman says, even if the law is interpreted fairly broadly. But Brookman says he hopes the case culminates in new privacy protections for internet users, as long as those new protections don’t place the burden on internet users.

“I think just a prohibition on sharing [personal data] would be a better result than forcing people through a million consent screens in every site they go to,” Brookman said.

A chilling effect

Tracking and sharing the histories of the videos people watch could negatively affect internet users’ behavior, according to Eric Null, director of the privacy and data project at the Center for Democracy and Technology.

“Watching videos is an expressive activity, and having those videos tracked, shared, and sold to third parties for various and potentially nefarious purposes will chill that expression,” Null said in an email to CNET.

“The VPPA does cover free online pre-recorded videos, but the statute nonetheless has significant limitations in its scope that can only be rectified by updating our privacy laws,” he said. “We could, of course, do so through a comprehensive privacy law that includes protections for video viewing.”

A Supreme Court ruling is expected in 2027.

Tech.title: Our Favorite Air Purifier Brand Just Released a Smaller, More Affordable Option
Tech.content:
Coway, the brand that nabbed the top two spots on CNET’s best air purifier list after our recent testing, just released a brand-new, compact unit that’s part of its popular Airmega lineup.

The Airmega Mighty2 Mini features ultra-quiet operation, a multi-stage filtration system and a compact design that’s 40% smaller than its larger counterpart, the Airmega Mighty2. But the price tag may be the biggest draw.

The top two picks on our list, the Airmega 450 and the Airmega 400S, retail for $499 and $680, respectively, while the Mighty2 retails for $270. Yet the Mighty2 Mini comes in as the most impressive steal at $170.

How the Airmega Mighty2 Mini works

I received the Airmega Mighty2 Mini ahead of its launch. Although our lab team in Louisville, Kentucky, hasn’t yet put it through our rigorous air purifier testing, a few things were clear off the bat. To start, this unit is cute. The sleek and compact design makes it ideal for any room, but its quiet operation makes it ideal for bedrooms and nurseries. The Airmega Mighty2 Mini is available in white, beige and green.

It has a manufacturer-listed range of 19.2 to 49 decibels, depending on the mode used. For reference, 49 decibels is comparable to moderate rainfall. When it was set to its lowest speed, I never noticed it was on, but at its highest, I could definitely hear it. However, it was still significantly quieter than my window air-conditioner unit or tower fan.

The Airmega Mighty2 Mini has four modes and three speeds. Corin Cesaric-Epple/CNETv

It has eco, turbo, sleep and smart modes, as well as three speeds, a timer option and a washable pre-filter, a carbon filter, and a HEPA filter that can remove 99.97% of particles 0.3 microns or larger. It weighs less than 10 pounds and is easy to move from room to room.

Unlike some other air purifiers, including some from Coway itself, this affordable option lacks app connectivity. Still, it has a simple built-in air quality monitor with a four-color LED indicator at the top of the unit that shows the air quality in your room at any given time.

Our lab tested the larger Airmega Mighty, and during the particle-removal test, it removed 90% of fine particles in 90 seconds with the fan on high and in 2 minutes and 45 seconds with the fan on low. Although these are decent results, other units, including the top two Coway options, outperformed it in particle-removal speed. Still, the prices of the Airmega Mighty options are hard to beat.

One of my favorite things about this unit is how easy it is to remove and replace the filters. Corin Cesaric-Epple/CNET

In our next round of air purifier testing, we will include the new Airmega Mighty2 Mini to see whether it can impress us as much as larger Airmega models.

Tech.title: Google Rolls Out Its Universal Cart Shopping Tool
Tech.content:
Google’s Universal Cart is rolling out across search and the Gemini app in the US, just ahead of Black Friday and the holiday shopping season.

Think less browser extension, more a way to shop within Google.

The Universal Cart is an AI-powered shopping tool that helps you stay on top of products you’re considering buying from a variety of retailers you encounter on Google. If you want to continue shopping later, Google will save your products and progress so you can pick up where you left off. The cart will refresh listings for over 60 billion products to keep an eye on price changes and low-stock alerts in Google’s Shopping Graph.

More from CNET

It can also alert you to price drops and when an item is back in stock.

Once you’ve narrowed your purchase, the Universal Cart — built on Google Wallet — can help you find promotional savings and choose which credit card reaps the most rewards. When you’re ready to buy, Google uses the Universal Commerce Protocol for checkout, and you can make purchases from your cart using Google Pay. Or you can move the items from Google to the merchant cart to finish your purchase. Your purchase confirmations and customer support will still come from the retailer.

However, there are some caveats. You’ll need to start through Google to shop, not the merchant’s website. It’s not quite a browser extension to add a button to every website you visit.

Meanwhile, Meta is touting the shopping capabilities of its newly introduced Muse AI agent.

Google previewed the Universal Cart in May at its I/O developer forum.

Tech.title: Grand Theft Auto 6: The Release Trailer You’ve Been Waiting For
Tech.content:
Rockstar Games is taking one of the last steps on a very long road: The Grand Theft Auto 6 launch trailer arrived Thursday. In an incredibly popular but chaotic series, the new trailer hits different from the rest, complete with a new, haunting track from Justice, featuring Tame Impala, SZA and King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard. We’re obsessed with it all.

Judging from the trailer, it seems like the wait has been worth it. The launch trailer hits a beat that the other games haven’t seemed to quite elevate to. It was almost a year ago that Rockstar Games announced it would be releasing GTA 6, and now we’re getting closer to its Nov. 19 release date for the Xbox Series X, Series S and PlayStation 5.

The story centers around a character named Jason, who used to be in the army, but admits he “got into some trouble,” and that they “don’t give loans to people like me.” When he gets a call from the other central character, Lucia, the story begins, and we’re swept into the adventure and chaos that this game is trying to bring to the table.

More from CNET

GTA has always been a choose-your-own-adventure type of game. Personally, I’ve never played through the storylines, instead preferring the open-world nature of doing anything you want in an extensive setting. But this trailer has me intrigued and wanting to know what happens to our main characters.

The new background track is dynamic and sad, suggesting that the story that will unfold won’t be your typical smash-and-bash game.

GTA 6 has been in development for an extremely long time — GTA 5 came out in 2013 — and we’re about to see just what the fruits of Rockstar Games’ labor are all about. Get ready for a new ride that should bring old GTA lovers and newcomers on board.

Tech.title: You Can Now Play Battlefield 6 and More on Xbox Game Pass
Tech.content:
Xbox Game Pass subscribers can jump into huge battles now in Battlefield 6. That’s good because, Microsoft removed one of CNET’s best games of 2025, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, from the service. Maybe Battlefield 6 and the other games arriving this month will have what it takes to fill the Clair Obscur-sized hole in my heart.

Xbox Game Pass, a CNET Editors’ Choice award pick, offers a wide selection of games you can play on your Xbox Series X, Xbox Series S, Xbox One and PC or mobile device for as little as $10 a month. With a subscription to the higher-tiered Game Pass Ultimate ($23 a month), you can access hundreds of games, including new ones the day they’re released, each month.

Here are all the games Microsoft is adding to Xbox Game Pass in the first half of October 2026.

More from CNET

Battlefield 6

Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play now.

CNET’s David Lumb called this installment in the popular Battlefield series a “riveting shooter.” It’s full of huge multiplayer battles, close-quarters combat and loads of gunfights and explosions. While most people will gravitate towards multiplayer, there is a single-player campaign if you want a break from the online mayhem.

Valor Mortis

Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play now.

In this first-person soulslike game, you’re a soldier in Napoleon’s army who dies. No worries, because you’re back from the dead with a handful of supernatural abilities that you wield in your left hand, like in the almost 20-year-old game BioShock. You’ll use these skills to battle monsters and uncover a conspiracy that could threaten all of humanity.

Bluey’s Happy Snaps

Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play now.

Bluey’s Happy Snaps proves that not every game coming to Game Pass has to be full of action. You’ll unwind and explore Bluey’s world while taking photos in areas familiar to anyone who’s seen the popular children’s show – let’s be honest, this show’s also popular with adults. You can take photos on your own, or play with a partner, friend or your kid as you turn in-game moments into fun.

Other games coming to Game Pass soon

Those are a few of the games Microsoft is bringing to Game Pass in October. Here are the rest of the games you’ll see on the service soon.

Echo Weaver: Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play now.

Forever Ago: Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play now.

Neon Abyss 2: Xbox Game Pass Ultimate, Game Pass Premium and PC Game Pass subscribers can play now.

Deep Dish Dungeon: Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play now.

Chained Beasts: Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play now.

Beyond These Stars: Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play on Oct. 16.

Games that left Xbox Game Pass

Microsoft also removed nine games from Xbox Game Pass, including the award-winning Clair Obscur. So you’ll have to buy these games separately now if you still want to play them.

For more on Xbox, check out our Xbox Game Pass review, learn which Game Pass plan is right for you and discover what other games you can play on the service.
